title: How to Deal with Jet Lag After Travel — and Why the First 48 Hours on the Riviera Matter
meta_title: How to Deal with Jet Lag After Travel | First 48h Riviera
meta_description: How to deal with jet lag after travel: light, meals, the nap rule — and one Reiki session in your hotel in the first 48 hours. Cannes, Riviera.
keyword: how to deal with jet lag after travel
body:
Jet lag is not tiredness. It is a disagreement between your body clock and the clock on the wall, and the two of them argue for as long as it takes the body to give in — usually one day for every time zone you crossed. The fastest way to deal with it is to give the body strong, clear signals about where it is now: daylight at the right hours, food at local times, and one long period of real rest in the first two days.

Most advice stops there, and it is good advice. What it leaves out is the part I see every week: the nervous system arrives more stressed than the body. After a long flight people are not just sleepy, they are wired — heart a little fast, mind a little loud, unable to nap even when they finally lie down. That state does not fix itself with a coffee on the Croisette.

This article gives you the practical checklist first, then the one thing I would add to it.

## The plain checklist for the first 48 hours

**Light.** Get outside in the morning on day one, even for twenty minutes. Daylight is the strongest signal your body clock has. If you arrived from the east, morning light pulls you forward; from the west, afternoon light works better. Either way: outside, not behind glass.

**Meals at local times.** Eat breakfast when the Riviera eats breakfast, even if you're not hungry. The digestive system is a second clock, and it listens.

**No big nap.** Twenty minutes is fine. Two hours in a dark room at 4 pm will cost you the night.

**Water, less alcohol.** The plane dried you out. The rosé on the terrace will not put it back.

**Move, gently.** A walk along the sea in Antibes does more than a workout. You want circulation, not another stressor.

Do these five things and most people feel normal by day three. The problem is the two days in between — and that is where most of a week's holiday, or a first week after a move, quietly goes.

## Why the body doesn't just switch off

A long flight is a long stretch of low-level alert: noise, dry air, no real sleep, a body held still in a seat for hours. By the time you reach your hotel the tiredness is there but so is a background hum that will not turn down. People describe it as "exhausted but can't sleep", or "I lay down and my brain kept going".

That hum is the sympathetic nervous system — the fight-or-flight side — still running at cruising altitude. Until it stands down, the rest signals you send (dark room, cool sheets) don't fully land. You can be doing everything right and still be awake at 3 am.

## What I add: one session in the first day or two

This is the reason the Arrival Reset exists. It is a 45-minute Reiki session in your hotel room or villa within 48 hours of landing. You lie down, fully clothed. I work with hands placed lightly on or just above the body, in a set sequence, without conversation. Most people go somewhere between deep rest and sleep within ten minutes.

What it does, in plain terms: it gives the nervous system a strong signal that it is safe to stand down — the same signal that a very good night's sleep gives, but delivered while you are still awake enough to receive it. People tend to sleep properly that night, and the checklist above starts working the way it is supposed to.

I will not tell you it resets your circadian rhythm; nothing does that in 45 minutes. It resets the *state* you are trying to fall asleep in, which is the thing that was actually blocking you.

## A note on timing

If you land at Nice airport on a Friday afternoon, Terminal 2 to a hotel in Cannes is about forty minutes on the A8. A session at 7 pm that evening, before dinner, is ideal. Second best is the next morning. By day three the window has mostly closed — you're through the worst of it on your own, and a session is still pleasant but no longer doing the job it was built for.

Reiki is complementary. It sits alongside whatever you already do for sleep and health, and does not replace medical advice if jet lag is severe or you have a condition that travel affects.

## FAQ

**How long does jet lag last after a long-haul flight?**
Roughly one day per time zone crossed, so a flight from New York to Nice usually means three to five days. Light, meals at local times and one properly restful night in the first 48 hours shorten it.

**Can a Reiki session on the day I land really help with jet lag?**
It won't change your body clock, but it settles the nervous system so the rest you need can actually happen. Most people sleep well that night, which is what shortens the rest of the adjustment.

**Where does an Arrival Reset session happen?**
In your hotel room, your rented villa, or on a yacht at anchor — anywhere on the Riviera from Saint-Tropez to Monaco. You need a quiet room and 45 minutes; I bring everything else.

## If you're landing soon

Message me on WhatsApp with your arrival day and where you're staying. Same-day and next-day slots are often possible, and the earlier in the first 48 hours we do it, the more of your week you get back. The Arrival Reset is €180, travel within Cannes, Antibes and Nice included.

title: Signs of Burnout: The Ones That Don't Look Like Burnout
meta_title: Signs of Burnout That Don't Look Like Burnout
meta_description: The signs of burnout most people miss — it rarely looks like collapse. What it looks like instead, and what helps when you can't stop. Cannes.
body:
The signs of burnout most people expect are collapse, tears, not being able to get out of bed. Those are the late signs. The early ones are quieter and much easier to explain away: you are efficient but joyless, you sleep but wake tired, you can do the work but not the small talk afterwards, and the thing you used to love about your job now produces a faint sense of dread on Sunday evening.

Burnout, in the plain definition, is exhaustion plus detachment plus a feeling that what you do no longer works. It is not a medical diagnosis in most countries; it is a state. And the early state looks less like breaking down than like running on a battery that never gets above forty percent.

Here are the signs I hear about most often from the people who come to me in Cannes — nearly all of them high-functioning, most of them convinced they were "just tired".

## Efficiency with the lights off

You are still getting things done. Emails answered, deals closed, children collected. From the outside nothing has changed. From the inside, every task feels like lifting the same weight twice. This is the sign people miss longest, because the output is intact. Only the cost has changed.

## Sleep that doesn't repair

You sleep six, seven, eight hours and wake up already behind. Or you fall asleep instantly and wake at 4 am with a mind that has been running while you slept. Burnout sleep is not insomnia exactly. It's sleep without the part where the body puts itself back together.

## Irritation at small things, flatness at big things

A slow waiter irritates you more than it should. A good piece of news lands with nothing. Both come from the same place: the nervous system has been in alert for so long that it has stopped modulating. Everything is either a threat or nothing.

## The body starts talking

Jaw tight in the morning. Shoulders up near the ears by lunchtime. A stomach that reacts to stress before your mind has registered it. Headaches at the end of the week. What I hear most often, in the first session, is a version of the same sentence: "I didn't know my shoulders were up until they came down." People have carried the hold for so long it has become their shape. The body reports burnout long before the person admits it.

## "I just need a holiday"

You take one. You come back. Within four days it is exactly the same. This is the clearest sign of all, and the one people argue with hardest. If rest doesn't restore you, you are not tired. Something has stopped doing its job — usually the ability to switch off at all.

## What helps when you can't stop

The honest answer is that burnout recovers when the nervous system learns it is allowed to stand down. A month in the mountains does that for some people. Most of the people I work with cannot take a month; they have a company, a family abroad, a household in a country that isn't theirs yet.

What I offer instead is a series of four sessions over three to five weeks — The Renewal. Each is 45 minutes, at your home or villa or at my space in Cannes. You lie down, fully clothed, and for the length of the session nothing is asked of you. That is not a metaphor. It is the whole point. Most people describe the first session as the first time in months their body was fully still. By the third or fourth, the stillness starts to be available outside the session too.

Reiki doesn't treat burnout — nothing external does. What it does is give the system a repeated, reliable experience of standing down, until it remembers how. If your burnout comes with symptoms a doctor should see — chest pain, persistent low mood, panic — see the doctor first. The sessions work alongside that, not instead of it.

## FAQ

**What are the first signs of burnout?**
Waking tired after enough sleep, losing pleasure in work you used to enjoy, irritation at small things and flatness at good news, and a holiday that doesn't restore you. Collapse comes much later, if at all.

**Is burnout the same as depression?**
No, though they can overlap. Burnout is tied to a specific load and usually lifts when the load and the nervous system are addressed. If your low mood doesn't lift with rest, or you feel hopeless, speak to a doctor.

**How does Reiki help with signs of burnout?**
By giving the nervous system a repeated experience of full rest, so it relearns how to switch off. It's complementary — it works alongside medical or psychological care, never instead.

title: Burnout Symptoms in Women: What Gets Missed
meta_title: Burnout Symptoms in Women: What Gets Missed
meta_description: Burnout symptoms in women often don't match the checklists. What it actually looks like when you hold a family, a job and a life abroad — and what helps.
body:
Burnout symptoms in women are missed for a simple reason: the checklists were written for a person whose load is visible. A job, a boss, a deadline. When the load is a job plus a household plus two children in a new school plus the invisible work of being the one who remembers everything, the exhaustion doesn't look like burnout. It looks like a woman who is coping.

The symptoms are the same at the root — exhaustion, detachment, the sense that effort no longer produces anything — but they show up differently. They show up as guilt, as a short temper with the people you love most, as a body that hurts in ways no scan explains, and as an inability to rest even when rest is finally available.

I work mostly with women who have moved to the Riviera for a partner's job, their own business, or a new chapter. Here is what burnout actually looks like in that life.

## Tired, but unable to sit down

The clearest sign. There is finally a free hour — children at school, husband in Monaco, house quiet — and you cannot use it. You tidy something. You answer three messages. You stand in the kitchen. The nervous system has been on duty so long it no longer recognises "off". Rest has become a task you're failing at.

## Guilt as the default feeling

Not enough with the children. Not enough at work. Not enough for the marriage, the parents back home, your own body. Burnout in women often wears guilt as its main costume, because the exhaustion gets read as a personal failure rather than a system running past capacity.

## The body carries it first

Cycle discomfort that got worse this year. Jaw pain. A stomach that knots at 6 pm. Headaches that arrive on Fridays. One client came to me for what she called "hormonal stuff" — sharp discomfort during her period that had become noticeably worse since the move. After one session she messaged that the discomfort that month was, in her words, noticeably easier. I don't claim Reiki did something to her cycle. I think her body finally had 45 minutes where nothing was being asked of it, and the difference showed up where the tension had been living.

## Snapping at the wrong people

You are patient with clients, teachers, the man at the préfecture. You snap at your partner and your children. This is not a character flaw. It is a nervous system with no reserves left, spending its last patience where it is required and running out where it is safe.

## "I'm fine, other people have it harder"

The sentence I hear most. It is usually true and completely beside the point. A system can be past capacity and still be luckier than most.

## What actually helps — and what doesn't

Advice for women in burnout tends to add tasks: journal, meditate, exercise, self-care. If you are already past capacity, a new task is a new weight. What helps is the opposite: an hour where you are the one being looked after and no one needs anything from you.

That is what a Reiki session is, stripped of anything mystical. You lie down, fully clothed, at home in Mougins or Cap d'Antibes while the children are at school, or at my space in Cannes. I work quietly for 45 minutes. You are not asked to relax, breathe correctly, or think of anything. Most women fall asleep. The ones who don't tell me they hadn't felt their own body without a to-do list running in years.

Four sessions over a month — The Renewal — is the shape I usually suggest, because the first session mostly shows the body what off feels like, and the next three let it practise.

None of this replaces a doctor. If the exhaustion comes with symptoms that worry you — heavy bleeding, persistent low mood, thyroid or heart questions — get them checked. The sessions work alongside that care, and the two are better together than either alone.

## FAQ

**What are the most common burnout symptoms in women?**
Being unable to rest even when time is available, constant guilt, a body that hurts in ways scans don't explain, short temper with family but patience with strangers, and "I'm fine" as a reflex.

**Why does burnout in women get missed?**
Because the load is invisible — household, children, emotional labour — and because the woman is still coping. The checklists look for collapse; women in burnout usually look competent.

**Can Reiki help with burnout in women?**
It gives the nervous system a reliable experience of being off duty, which is what burnout takes away. It's a complementary practice — alongside a doctor when there are physical symptoms, never instead of one.

title: Wired and Tired: When Your Nervous System Won't Stand Down
meta_title: Wired and Tired: When the Nervous System Won't Stand Down
meta_description: Anxious for no reason, exhausted but can't switch off: what "wired and tired" is, why it follows a move, and what settles it. Cannes.
body:
Wired and tired is the state where you are exhausted and cannot switch off at the same time. You lie down and your mind keeps running. You sit on the terrace and your leg bounces. You are anxious for no reason you can point to, and the anxiety has no object — it is just there, in the chest, in the jaw, in the way you check your phone without wanting to.

The plain explanation: your nervous system won't stand down. The sympathetic branch — fight or flight — has been on for so long that "on" has become its resting state. The parasympathetic branch, the one that governs digestion, sleep and repair, isn't getting a turn. You can be safe, on holiday, in one of the most beautiful places in Europe, and your body is still scanning for the thing that is going to go wrong.

This isn't a diagnosis. It's a pattern, and it is by far the most common one I see in Cannes among people who have recently moved, recently sold a company, or recently stopped moving after years of movement.

## Why safe places don't feel safe

The system that keeps you alert doesn't know the difference between a real threat and a long list of small ones. Relocation is a long list of small ones: the bank, the school, the language, the car, the paperwork, the friends you haven't made yet. None of it is dangerous. All of it is unresolved. Unresolved is what the alert system feeds on.

Then you arrive at the point where the list is mostly done — the villa in Le Cannet is furnished, the children are settled — and you expect to feel relief. Instead you feel nothing, or you feel worse. The body has been in a posture of readiness for months and doesn't have a "list finished" signal. It only has "still on".

## The signs it's your nervous system and not your life

- You can't nap even when you're desperate to
- You wake between 3 and 5 am, alert, with nothing specific wrong
- Small noises make you flinch; small decisions feel large
- Your shoulders are near your ears and you didn't notice
- Rest makes you more restless, not less

If your life were the problem, fixing the life would fix the feeling. When it's the nervous system, the life can be fixed and the feeling stays. That is the tell.

## What settles it

Not thinking. You cannot reason a nervous system down; it doesn't speak that language. It responds to bodily signals of safety: stillness, warmth, slow breath, another person's calm attention held on you for long enough that the body believes it.

This is why a Reiki session works for wired-and-tired people even when they are the last person who would believe in energy work. It is 45 minutes of exactly those signals, with nothing asked of you. You lie down, fully clothed. My hands rest lightly on or just above the body in a set sequence. There is no conversation, no instruction to relax, no breathing to get right. The body is simply given, for 45 minutes, every reason to stand down — and most of the time, somewhere around minute ten, it does.

People describe it afterwards in almost the same words: "I didn't know I was that tense until it stopped." Sleep that night is usually different. One session shows the body what off feels like. Whether you need more depends on how long it has been on.

I won't promise this fixes anything. If the anxiety is severe, has a specific trigger, or comes with panic, speak to a doctor or therapist first — this works alongside that, not instead. What I can say is what I see every week: a system that has forgotten how to stand down can be reminded, and it usually remembers faster than people expect.

## FAQ

**What does "wired and tired" mean?**
It's the state of being exhausted and unable to switch off at the same time — a nervous system stuck in alert even when there's nothing to be alert about. Common after relocation, a long work push or a hard year.

**Why can't I relax even on holiday?**
Because the nervous system doesn't have a "holiday" signal. It has "on" and "off", and after months of unresolved small stresses, "on" becomes its default. It needs bodily signals of safety to change, not a change of scenery.

**How does Reiki help a nervous system that won't stand down?**
A session is 45 minutes of stillness, warmth and calm attention with nothing asked of you — the exact signals the parasympathetic system responds to. It's complementary; if anxiety is severe, see a doctor first.

## If this is you right now

One session is enough to find out whether this is the thing. Message me on WhatsApp — I'm in Cannes, and I come to Antibes, Nice and the villages behind them. A single session is €180.

title: Distance Reiki: How It Works, Step by Step (and Why I Use a Proxy)
meta_title: Distance Reiki: How It Works Step by Step
meta_description: How does distance Reiki work? The same 45-minute session without the geography — what you do, the proxy I use, what people report.
body:
Distance Reiki works like this: we agree a time on WhatsApp; you lie down wherever you are; I give the full 45-minute session from Cannes, working on a stand-in for your body; I message you when it's done. The sequence, the length and the attention are the same as an in-person session. Only the location changes.

That's the whole mechanism from your side. The rest of this article explains what happens on mine, why the practice exists in the Reiki tradition at all, and what people actually report — because "sending energy" is not a phrase I use, and I'd rather you understood the thing than took my word for it.

## Where distance practice comes from

Usui Reiki has three degrees. The second degree — the level I hold — introduces three symbols, and one of them exists specifically for working without physical contact, across distance and time. This isn't a modern add-on for the internet age; it was taught this way in Japan in the 1920s. Practitioners have been giving sessions to people in other cities for a century.

So when I offer a distance session, I'm not improvising. I'm doing a defined practice, in a defined way, that has a defined place in the tradition I trained in.

## What I actually do — the proxy

Here is the part most practitioners don't explain, and the part I think matters most.

I don't sit in a room and "send" something into the air. I work on a physical stand-in for your body — a proxy. For those 45 minutes it becomes you. My hands move over it exactly as they would over you if you were on the table in front of me: head, throat, chest, stomach, lower body, in the same order, at the same pace, unhurried. The session has a beginning, a middle and an end, and my attention is on you the whole way through.

If that sounds strange, consider how you already use proxies: the photo of someone that makes you feel close to them; the chair they always sat in. The mind and body are very good at treating a representation as the thing. The proxy gives my hands somewhere to be and my attention something to hold. What you receive is the attention.

## What you do

1. **Agree a time.** Any time zone. If you're in London, Dubai or on a plane tomorrow, we find a slot that's quiet at your end.
2. **Lie down.** Hotel bed, sofa, a reclined seat — anywhere you won't be disturbed. Phone on silent. Fully clothed, obviously.
3. **45 minutes.** Rest, doze, or simply notice. There is nothing to do and nothing to get right.
4. **A message from me** when it's done, and a short exchange about what you noticed.

## What people report

I'll tell you what I hear, and I'll tell you honestly what I don't know.

Many people tell me afterwards that they felt warmth, or a kind of pressure, in the exact places my hands were — without knowing the sequence in advance. Some feel heavy, then very light. Some fall asleep within minutes and wake when the message arrives. A few feel very little during and notice the difference the next day, in how they slept.

I cannot give you a laboratory explanation for the first of those. I can tell you it is the most common thing people say, that they say it in Cannes and in Dubai, and that I stopped being surprised by it a long time ago.

## Who it's for

People who travel — a founder living between Nice and London, a family that winters here and summers elsewhere. People who've just landed and want the session before they're ready to have anyone in the room. People who simply prefer to receive without being seen. And people who've already had sessions in person and want to keep the rhythm going when they're away.

It isn't a lesser version. For some people it is the better one.

Reiki is a complementary practice in any form; a distance session doesn't replace medical or psychological care, and I'll say so if something you describe needs a doctor first.

## FAQ

**How does distance Reiki work?**
We agree a time, you lie down wherever you are, and I give the full 45-minute session working on a proxy for your body, in the same sequence I'd use in person. I message you when it's done.

**What is a proxy in distance Reiki?**
A physical stand-in for your body that my hands work over during the session. It gives the practice structure and my attention something to hold; what you receive is the attention.

**Does distance Reiki feel the same as in person?**
Many people report the same sensations — warmth or pressure where my hands were, heaviness, deep rest. Some feel less during and more the next day. Both are normal.

title: Is Reiki Dangerous? What Doctors Actually Say
meta_title: Is Reiki Dangerous? What Doctors Actually Say
meta_description: Is Reiki dangerous? No — no physical risk, no side effects beyond tiredness. The one real danger is using it instead of a doctor.
body:
No. Reiki is not dangerous. There is no known physical risk from a session: no substance enters the body, no force is applied, nothing is manipulated. Hands rest lightly on or just above a fully clothed body for 45 minutes. The most anyone reports afterwards is feeling very tired, very emotional for an evening, or thirsty. That is the honest, complete answer to the question, and doctors who have looked at Reiki say the same thing: whatever it does or doesn't do, it doesn't harm.

The reason people search "is reiki dangerous" — and in France it's one of the most common Reiki searches — isn't usually about the session. It's about what surrounds it: claims, money, and whether they'll be talked out of seeing a doctor. Those are fair worries, and they deserve a straight answer too.

## What doctors say

The medical position, stated plainly, is this: Reiki has not been shown in controlled studies to treat any disease; it has also not been shown to cause harm; and it produces relaxation, which is useful. That is why some hospitals in the US and UK allow Reiki volunteers on wards — not because it cures anything, but because calm patients do better and it costs nothing in risk.

Where doctors become critical is when a practitioner tells a patient to stop treatment. That is the danger. Not the session — the advice around it.

## The one real danger

If someone offers you Reiki *instead of* medical care for something serious, walk away. That is the only situation where Reiki becomes dangerous, and the danger is entirely in the substitution.

I say this on my homepage and I'll say it here: I work alongside your doctors, never instead of them. If you tell me about a symptom that needs a doctor, I'll tell you to see one before we book. Reiki is complementary. It sits next to care; it isn't care.

## What you might feel afterwards

- **Tired.** The most common. The body has been in deep rest and wants more of it. Sleep that night is usually good.
- **Emotional.** Some people cry during or after, without a clear reason. It passes by the next day and most describe it as relief rather than distress.
- **Thirsty, slightly headachy.** Rare, brief, and the same thing you'd feel after a massage. Water fixes it.
- **Nothing.** Also normal. Some people feel the difference in how they sleep rather than in the session.

None of these are side effects in the medical sense. They are what a nervous system does when it stands down for the first time in a while.

## Who should check first

If you're pregnant, have a pacemaker, are in cancer treatment, or have a psychiatric condition, tell your doctor you're planning a Reiki session. Not because Reiki is known to interfere with any of these — it isn't — but because your doctor should know what's around your care, and because I'd rather you had that conversation than wondered.

## Why it's safe to try once

The session in Cannes or at your villa asks nothing of you but 45 minutes lying down. You don't need to believe anything. You don't take anything. If nothing happens, you've had a long rest in the middle of the day, which is not a bad outcome on the Riviera. If something happens, you'll know, and you can decide from there.

## FAQ

**Is Reiki dangerous?**
No. There is no known physical risk from a session. The only real danger is using Reiki instead of medical care for something serious — which I never advise.

**Does Reiki have side effects?**
Not in the medical sense. Some people feel tired, emotional or thirsty for a few hours afterwards; it passes by the next day. Some feel nothing during and notice better sleep after.

**What do doctors think of Reiki?**
That it hasn't been shown to treat disease, hasn't been shown to cause harm, and produces relaxation. Doctors object when practitioners advise stopping treatment — which is the line I never cross.

title: How to Manage Emotional Burnout When You Can't Take a Month Off
meta_title: How to Manage Emotional Burnout Without Stopping
meta_description: How to manage emotional burnout without a month off — what to drop, what to keep, and four Reiki sessions that give the body its own time off.
body:
The standard advice for emotional burnout is to stop. Take leave, go somewhere quiet, do nothing for a month. It is good advice for the few people who can follow it. For everyone else — the ones with a company that doesn't run without them, or two children in an international school in Mougins, or parents to call in another country every evening — it lands as one more thing they're failing to do.

So here is the other version: how to manage emotional burnout inside a full life, without a month off. It's less dramatic and it works.

## First, name what emotional burnout actually is

Physical burnout is a tired body. Emotional burnout is a tired *capacity to care*. You still love the people; you just have nothing left to give them at 7 pm. You still believe in the work; you just feel nothing when it goes well. The reserve that makes feelings possible has been drawn down to zero, and every demand on it comes back as irritation, flatness or guilt.

That reserve refills in one condition only: when nothing is being asked of it. Which is exactly what a full life never provides.

## Drop, don't add

Most burnout advice adds things. Journal. Meditate twenty minutes. Exercise. Gratitude. If you have nothing left, a new practice is a new demand. Start instead by removing:

- **One recurring obligation** that exists only because it always has. The weekly call, the group chat, the thing you host.
- **The phone in the bedroom.** Not forever. For three weeks.
- **Being the one who remembers.** Hand one category of family admin to someone else, entirely, even if they do it worse.

None of this is Reiki. It's the ground the sessions stand on.

## Give the nervous system its own time off

Here is the honest mechanism. Emotional burnout persists because the nervous system never gets a signal that the demand has stopped. Even when you're alone, you're braced. A month away works because eventually — usually around day ten — the body stops bracing.

A session does the same thing in 45 minutes, four times, instead of thirty days once. You lie down, fully clothed, at home or at my space in Cannes. Nothing is asked of you: not to relax, not to breathe a certain way, not to talk. My hands rest lightly on or above the body and stay there. Somewhere in the first ten minutes, most people feel the bracing let go — the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach. That release is the nervous system getting its signal.

Once is a glimpse. Four times over a month — The Renewal — is enough for the body to start expecting it, and for the reserve to begin refilling between sessions rather than draining.

## What one client noticed

A woman I worked with described her state before the first session as "I just want to lie down all day". She wasn't ill; she'd checked. She'd simply run out. After the second session she said she'd found herself wanting to cook, which she hadn't in months. By the fourth she was talking about a project. I don't take credit for the project. I think the wanting came back when the emptiness stopped being maintained.

## What to expect and not expect

Expect sleep to change first. Expect to feel more, not less, for a few days — emotional burnout numbs, and un-numbing is uncomfortable before it's good. Expect the flatness to lift unevenly.

Don't expect four sessions to undo two years. Don't expect it to work if the load itself is impossible — sometimes the honest answer is that something has to be taken off the table, and no session changes that.

And if the burnout comes with persistent low mood, hopelessness or panic, see a doctor. Reiki is complementary. It works alongside that care; it doesn't replace it.

## FAQ

**How do you manage emotional burnout without taking time off?**
Remove one obligation, get the phone out of the bedroom, hand off one category of admin — and give the nervous system a reliable, repeated experience of nothing being asked of it. That's what the sessions provide.

**What's the difference between emotional and physical burnout?**
Physical burnout is a tired body; emotional burnout is a depleted capacity to feel and care. You can be physically rested and still emotionally empty.

title: What Does a Reiki Session Feel Like? An Honest Description
meta_title: What Does a Reiki Session Feel Like? Honest Answer
meta_description: What does a Reiki session feel like? Warmth, heaviness, deep rest — and sometimes nothing at all. An honest description from a practitioner in Cannes.
keyword: what does a reiki session feel like
body:
A Reiki session feels, for most people, like falling into a very deep rest while still slightly awake. The most common sensations are warmth where the hands are, a heaviness in the limbs that turns into lightness, and a sense of time going strange — 45 minutes that feels like ten. A good number of people simply fall asleep. Some feel very little during and notice the difference afterwards, in how they slept that night. All of these are normal.

That's the direct answer. The rest of this is the detail people ask me for before their first session in Cannes, because "relaxing" doesn't tell you much and they'd like to know what they're walking into.

## The first ten minutes

You lie down, fully clothed, on a table or a bed. I start at the head. Most people are still thinking at this point — about the day, about whether they're doing it right, about whether anything is happening. That's fine. There's nothing to do. Somewhere between minute five and minute ten, the thinking usually slows on its own. People describe it as the moment they "dropped". The jaw softens. The breath gets longer without being told to.

## Warmth, pressure, weight

The most reported sensation is warmth from the hands — more than you'd expect from hands at rest. Some people feel it as pressure, or as a kind of pull, in places I'm not touching. Some feel the whole body get heavy, like sinking into the table, and then at some point very light. A few see colours behind closed eyes. A few feel tingling in the hands or feet.

I don't interpret any of this for you and I'd be wary of anyone who does. These are things the body does when it stands down. They're worth noticing; they don't need decoding.

## The middle

By now most people are somewhere between sleep and waking. Time stops behaving. People who were sure they'd stayed awake the whole session are surprised when I tell them it's over. Some cry quietly for no reason they can name and feel better for it. Some snore. Both are fine. I keep working through either.

## Coming back

I finish at the feet. You'll feel me step back. I let you lie for a minute before saying anything, because coming up too fast from that depth is unpleasant. Then you sit up slowly. People are often a bit disoriented, in a pleasant way, and thirsty. We talk briefly about what you noticed, if you want to. You're never asked to report an experience you didn't have.

## When nothing happens

Sometimes people feel very little during the session — a bit of warmth, some rest, no drama. They're disappointed. Then they message me the next morning to say they slept eight hours straight for the first time in months. The session did its work; it just did it later, and in the place that mattered.

One client, Elena, wrote to me the day after: she'd spent the whole day before the session in bed with no energy at all, and afterwards felt, in her word, recharged. She hadn't felt anything dramatic on the table. The difference was in the day after.

## What it doesn't feel like

It doesn't hurt. Nothing is manipulated. There's no incense you didn't ask for, no chanting, no crystals on your chest. You're not asked to visualise anything or believe anything. If you're analytical by nature — most of my clients are — you can lie there thinking "this is nonsense" for 45 minutes and the session will still do what it does. The body doesn't require your agreement.

Reiki is complementary. It's a relaxation practice that works alongside medical care, not a treatment for anything.

## FAQ

**What does Reiki feel like during a session?**
Usually warmth where the hands rest, heaviness that turns into lightness, and deep rest that blurs time. Many people fall asleep. Some feel very little during and notice better sleep afterwards.

**Is it normal to feel nothing during Reiki?**
Yes. Some people's nervous systems are slow to stand down, and the effect shows up in sleep or mood the next day rather than on the table.

**Do you have to believe in Reiki for it to work?**
No. You can be entirely sceptical and the body still responds to 45 minutes of stillness and attention. Most of my clients are analytical by profession.

## If you'd like to find out what it feels like for you

One session, €180, at my space in Cannes or at your home. Message me on WhatsApp; I'll tell you what to expect for your situation specifically.

title: Parental Burnout Abroad: Raising Kids in a Country That Isn't Yours
meta_title: Parental Burnout Abroad: Kids in a Country Not Yours
meta_description: Parental burnout is heavier abroad — no village, no language, no grandparents nearby. What it looks like on the Riviera and what helps.
body:
Parental burnout is the state where you love your children and have nothing left to give them. It's not a bad day; it's a floor you don't come up from. The signs are exhaustion that sleep doesn't touch, going through the motions of care without feeling it, irritation you're ashamed of, and the sense that you've lost the parent you used to be.

Abroad, it's heavier, and for reasons that have nothing to do with the children. At home there is a village, even a thin one: grandparents forty minutes away, a friend who'll take one child for an afternoon, a school system you understand, a doctor you've known for years. On the Riviera, for most international families, there's none of that. There's you, your partner, and a country whose systems you're learning in a second language while also being the only stable thing your children have.

I work with a lot of families in Mougins, Valbonne and Cap d'Antibes who moved for a job, a business or a better life for the children. Nearly every parent I see is doing well by any outside measure, and nearly every one is closer to empty than they'll say.

## Why abroad is different

Three things go missing when you raise children in a country that isn't yours:

**The village.** Nobody takes the children for an afternoon. Every hour of childcare is either you, your partner, or paid.

**The reflexes.** At home you know which doctor, which school, which form. Here every task has a research phase first. Small things cost more.

**The witness.** The people who knew you before — who'd notice you're not yourself and say so — are in another time zone.

Burnout gets missed because the parent is still coping. The children are fed, at school, loved. The cost is invisible from outside and increasingly invisible from inside, because the parent has stopped having the spare attention to notice.

## What it looks like

- Dreading the 4 pm school pickup, not because of the children but because of what comes after
- Snapping, then crying about snapping, then snapping again
- Sleeping badly even when the children sleep through
- A body that aches — jaw, shoulders, stomach — with no obvious cause
- Losing the ability to enjoy the good moments while they're happening

## What helps — and doesn't

Advice for burnt-out parents usually adds tasks: self-care, date nights, exercise. If you're empty, each one is another thing to fail at. What actually helps is an hour where you are the one being looked after and no one needs you.

That's what I offer. A 45-minute session at your home while the children are at school — you lie down, fully clothed, and for the length of it nothing is asked of you. Not to relax, not to talk, not to think of anything. Most parents fall asleep within minutes. The first time, I'm often told, is the first time in months they've been horizontal without listening for someone.

Four of those over a month — The Renewal — is what I usually suggest. One shows the body what off feels like. The next three let it practise until some of that stillness is available at 6 pm too.

One more thing: this works for children as well, in a shorter, gentler form, and I've seen a child who hadn't slept through the night in months begin to — but that's a separate conversation, and always alongside their paediatrician. Start with yourself. A settled parent does more for a household than any amount of settling done to the children.

If your exhaustion comes with persistent low mood, hopelessness, or thoughts that frighten you, talk to a doctor. Reiki is complementary; it works alongside that care, never instead.

## The 4 pm problem, specifically

Most parents I work with describe the same hour: school pickup. Not because of the children but because of what follows — homework in a language you're learning alongside them, dinner, bath, the negotiation about screens, and then the evening you had planned to have for yourself, which you no longer have the energy for. A session in the morning, while the house is empty, is aimed at that hour. Not to make 4 pm easier; to make sure you arrive at it with something left.

## FAQ

**What is parental burnout?**
Exhaustion, emotional distance from your children, and loss of the parent you used to be — a floor you don't come up from, rather than a bad week. It's common and it's not a character failure.

**Why is parental burnout worse for expat families?**
No village, no grandparents nearby, every system in a second language, and no one around who knew you before. The load is heavier and the support thinner.

**Can Reiki help with parental burnout?**
It gives an exhausted parent an hour where nothing is asked of them, repeatedly, until the nervous system remembers how to rest. It's complementary — alongside a doctor if there are physical or mood symptoms.

title: Reiki for Skeptics: You Don't Have to Believe in Anything
meta_title: Reiki for Skeptics: No Belief Required
meta_description: Reiki for skeptics — what a session is without the mystical language, why analytical people respond, and how to test it in one hour.
body:
This is Reiki for skeptics, written by someone who works mostly with them. I'll start with what I won't tell you. I won't tell you Reiki channels universal energy through my hands, that it clears your chakras, or that it works because we're all connected. Those are ways of talking about it that some practitioners find true and useful. For a skeptic they are the reason you never booked.

Here is what I will tell you: a Reiki session is 45 minutes of lying still, fully clothed, while another person holds calm, unhurried attention on your body with hands resting lightly on or above it. Nothing is applied, taken, or manipulated. And the nervous system — the part of you that decides whether to be alert or at rest — responds to exactly those conditions, whether or not the mind approves.

Most of my clients in Cannes are founders, investors, lawyers, engineers. Analytical by trade, sceptical by habit. They come because something isn't working — sleep, energy, the ability to switch off — and they've tried the things they believe in. They stay because something changes. Not because they converted.

## What I think is happening

I'm a second-degree practitioner, not a physiologist, so take this as an informed opinion. The body has two settings: alert and rest. Alert is for threat and effort; rest is for repair, digestion and sleep. Modern life, and relocation in particular, keeps most people in alert far longer than the body was built for. Rest becomes something you fall into from exhaustion rather than something you can enter.

A session gives the body every signal that rest is safe: stillness, warmth, slow steady contact, another human's undivided calm attention, no demand of any kind. Held for long enough — usually around ten minutes — the body takes the signal. That's the drop people describe. Everything after it is the body doing what it does when it's finally allowed to.

Does Reiki add something beyond that? I think so. I can't prove it, and I don't need you to agree. The mechanism above is enough to explain most of what people report, and it requires no belief at all.

## What I don't know

I don't know why many people feel warmth or pressure in places I'm not touching. I don't know why some people sleep differently for a week after one session. I've stopped pretending to. I'd rather tell you what I see and let you test it than build a theory you'd have to accept first.

## How to test it like a skeptic

1. **Book one session, not a package.** €180. You're gathering data, not committing.
2. **Don't try to feel anything.** Lie there thinking "this is nonsense" if you like. The body doesn't need your cooperation.
3. **Track two things** for the 48 hours after: how you slept, and how easily you got irritated. Those are the earliest, most measurable shifts.
4. **Decide from that**, not from the session itself. The session may feel like a pleasant rest and nothing more. The night after is the data.

One client — analytical, running a fund from Cap d'Antibes — told me afterwards he'd spent the first twenty minutes mentally drafting an email. He couldn't remember the last twenty-five. He slept nine hours. He came back, and he still doesn't believe in energy work. That's fine with me.

## What I'll never ask of you

To believe. To visualise. To say "yes" out loud to receive. To buy a package before you've had a session. To stop seeing your doctor — Reiki is complementary, it sits alongside medical care and doesn't replace anything.

## FAQ

**Does Reiki work if you don't believe in it?**
Yes. The body responds to stillness, warmth and calm attention regardless of what the mind thinks. Most of my clients are sceptics; the results they report don't depend on belief.

**What is Reiki, without the mystical language?**
Forty-five minutes of lying still while a practitioner holds calm, unhurried attention on your body with light hand contact. The nervous system reads it as safety and stands down.

**How should a skeptic try Reiki?**
Book one session, don't try to feel anything, and track sleep and irritability for the next 48 hours. Judge by the data, not by the hour itself.

## If you'd like to test it

One session, €180, at my space in Cannes or at your home. Message me on WhatsApp. Bring your scepticism; it doesn't get in the way.

title: How Many Reiki Sessions Do You Need? An Honest Answer

How many Reiki sessions do you need? One tells you whether Reiki is for you. Three to four, spaced over a month, is where most people feel a clear shift. Eight, over two to three months, is for a longer-standing pattern you're ready to work through properly. And you are done when you no longer think about booking the next one — not when a package runs out.

That's the honest answer. Here's the reasoning, so you can decide for yourself rather than take a package because it was offered.

## Why not just one?

One session does something real: most people sleep better that night and feel the stillness for a day or two. But the nervous system learns by repetition. If it has been in alert for months, one experience of standing down is a glimpse, not a habit. By the third or fourth session the body starts to expect the drop — it happens faster, goes deeper, and lasts longer between sessions. That's the point where people say things like "I noticed my shoulders were down on their own on Tuesday."

So: one to find out. Three or four to change something.

## When four is right

A specific season — a relocation, a launch, a recovery, a hard few months you're coming out of. Something with a shape. Four sessions over three to five weeks (The Renewal) matches that shape. Most of my clients in Cannes start here.

## When eight is right

A pattern older than the season. Years of not switching off. A body that has been braced since before you can remember. Grief that's had no room. Eight sessions over two to three months (The Immersion) is a container long enough for the body to trust the change, and I check in with you as we go — if you're done at six, we stop at six.

## When one is enough

You've just landed and want to sleep tonight. You have a big week and want to arrive in it steady. You're curious and want data before deciding anything. One session — €180 — is exactly right, and I'll never push a package on someone who came for one.

## How to tell when you're done

You stop feeling that you need it. The stillness you found on the table is available on the terrace. You sleep. You can sit for an hour without reaching for the phone. At that point some people come once a month as maintenance; most simply stop and come back when the next season arrives. Both are correct.

## What I won't say

I won't tell you a number without knowing you. I won't tell you that more is always better; it isn't. And I won't tell you Reiki does what a doctor does — it's a complementary practice that works alongside medical care, and if you describe something that needs a doctor first, I'll say so before we book anything.

## Spacing matters more than number

Four sessions in four consecutive days do less than four across four weeks. The body needs the days between to practise what it learned on the table — to find the drop on its own, to sleep, to notice the shoulders are down. A week apart is the rhythm I suggest; ten days if life is full. Longer than a fortnight and the thread starts to loosen. If you're only here a week, three sessions across it works — that's Your Week Here — and if you're here for a month, weekly is right.

## FAQ

**How many Reiki sessions do you need to feel a difference?**
Most people notice better sleep after one. A clear, lasting shift usually shows by the third or fourth session, spaced a week or so apart.

**How often should Reiki sessions be?**
Weekly, or every ten days, while working through something — close enough that the body remembers. Monthly as maintenance if you want it. Never so often that it becomes a chore.

**Is one Reiki session enough?**
For a reset — after a flight, before a big week — yes. For a pattern that's been there for months, one is the beginning, not the whole.

A child who'd been waking most nights for months after a move began, after a few sessions, to sleep through — the parent's message was simply that he'd slept the night. ## What it's for, plainly

- Settling at bedtime and staying asleep
- The first weeks of a new school
- Big feelings that come out sideways — meltdowns, clinginess, stomach aches with no cause
- A child who is "fine" all day and falls apart at 6 pm

Anything a doctor should see. If your child has persistent stomach pain, fever, real sleep disorders, or anxiety that's stopping normal life, see the paediatrician first. I'll ask about this before we book. Reiki is complementary — it's the calm around the care, not the care.

## The parent, first

Honestly: the most useful session in a stressed household is usually the parent's. A settled adult does more for a child's nervous system than anything I do in fifteen minutes. If you're the one holding everything, start there — and then, if it makes sense, we do the child.

## FAQ

**Is Reiki safe for children?**
Yes. It's light hand contact with a parent present, nothing applied or manipulated. It works alongside your paediatrician, never instead — I'll ask about medical care before we book.

**How long is a Reiki session for a child?**
Fifteen to twenty-five minutes, depending on age and how they settle. Longer than that and a child is done; the short version is the right version.

It can help a small nervous system that's stuck in alert to settle at bedtime. One family saw their child begin sleeping through after a few sessions. Always alongside the paediatrician.

A cabin is ideal — quiet, shaded, cool. A shaded aft deck works if the boat is calm and the crew aren't working nearby. What doesn't work is the saloon with people passing through; the session needs an hour without interruption, and so do you.

Yes — at anchor or moored, in a cabin or on a shaded deck. A tender from the port collects me, or I walk on if you're in a marina. I bring nothing but myself.

**Does the boat's movement affect a Reiki session?**

€180 for 45 minutes, the same as on land. Tender pickup from Cannes or Antibes is included; further along the coast we agree a small travel addition.

body:
Feeling out of place after moving abroad is usually treated as a mindset problem — homesickness, adjustment, something to think your way through. It isn't, or not only. It is a body that hasn't arrived yet. You can be six months into a life in Antibes, with the house furnished and the children in school, and still feel like a visitor in your own kitchen. That is not a failure to adapt. It's a nervous system that has not received enough proof that this is home.

I moved here from elsewhere too. I know the specific tiredness of building a life in a language and a system that aren't yours, and I know how long the body takes to believe it's landed — much longer than the mind does. This article is about that gap, and what closes it.

## What dislocation actually is

When you move countries, everything that used to be automatic becomes a decision. Where to buy bread. How to speak to the pharmacist. Which side of the road the post box is on. Individually these are nothing. Collectively they mean the alert system is on all day, every day, for months — low-level, constant, exhausting.

The mind adapts to this in weeks. The body doesn't. The body keeps a posture of readiness until something tells it, physically, that it can stop. Nice weather doesn't do that. A beautiful view doesn't do that. Furniture arriving doesn't do that.

## How it shows up

- You're "settled" by every external measure and still feel like you're waiting for something
- You sleep, but wake with a low hum of unease
- Small tasks — the bank, the préfecture — cost more than they should
- You're more tired at 6 pm than you've ever been
- You feel a version of homesick that isn't about missing home; it's about not being anywhere

One thing I hear a lot: "I don't understand, everything is fine." That's the sentence. Everything is fine and the body doesn't know it yet.

## What doesn't help

Pushing through. Forcing yourself to join things. Deciding to feel at home. These are mind solutions to a body problem, and they add effort to a system that's already at capacity. The body doesn't take orders. It takes evidence.

## What helps: evidence, repeated

The body believes it's safe when it gets bodily signals of safety, over and over, until they outnumber the signals of alert. Stillness. Warmth. Being cared for without having to organise it. Sleep that goes deep.

That is what a Reiki session provides, stripped of any other language. Forty-five minutes at your home — the very home that doesn't feel like yours yet — lying down, fully clothed, with nothing asked of you. Hands resting lightly on the body in a set sequence. Most people go into deep rest within ten minutes. What the body registers is: here, in this place, I was safe for an hour. Do that four times over a month, and "here" starts to mean something to the body that it didn't before.

I'd suggest The Renewal — four sessions over three to five weeks — for exactly this, because the change I'm describing is cumulative. One session is a good afternoon. Four is a body that starts to arrive.

None of this replaces the actual work of settling — the language, the friends, the routines. And if the out-of-place feeling comes with persistent low mood, isolation you can't break, or anxiety that's stopping normal life, talk to a doctor. Reiki is complementary; it works alongside that, not instead.

## FAQ

**Why do I feel out of place after moving abroad even though everything is fine?**
Because the mind adapts in weeks and the body in months. Your nervous system is still in the alert posture it took on during the move, and it needs bodily evidence — not reasoning — that it can stand down.

**How long does it take to feel at home after moving abroad?**
Typically six months to two years, and it varies by person. Anything that gives the body repeated experiences of safety in the new place shortens it.

**Can Reiki help with adjusting after relocation?**
It gives the body repeated experiences of deep rest and safety in the new home, which is what "arriving" physically is. Complementary — alongside the practical work of settling, and alongside a doctor if mood is affected.

## If you've been here a while and still haven't landed

The Renewal is four sessions, €640, at your home. Message me on WhatsApp and tell me how long you've been here. I moved too; I'll understand the answer.

title: Reiki vs Massage: Which One Do You Actually Need?
meta_title: Reiki vs Massage: Which Do You Actually Need?
meta_description: Reiki vs massage — one works the muscles, the other the nervous system. When you need which, whether you can have both, and costs in Cannes.
body:
Massage works the muscles. Reiki works the nervous system. That's the difference in one line, and it tells you which to book: if the problem is a tight body — knots, stiffness, a sore back from the flight — you want massage. If the problem is a tight *state* — can't switch off, can't sleep, anxious with nothing to be anxious about — you want Reiki. If it's both, and it often is, you can have both; they don't compete.

People ask me this before their first session in Cannes more than any other question, usually because they've had massages that helped for a day and are wondering whether this is the same thing in different clothes. It isn't. Here's the plain comparison.

## What happens on the table

**Massage:** you undress, lie under a towel, and a therapist applies pressure and movement to muscle and tissue. It's physical work on you. You feel it; sometimes it hurts a little in a good way. The effect is mechanical — circulation, release of tension in specific muscles, sometimes a lot of relaxation as a by-product.

**Reiki:** you stay fully clothed. Hands rest lightly on or just above the body in a set sequence and stay there. No pressure, no movement. It feels like almost nothing is being done, and then somewhere around minute ten the body drops into a rest deeper than most people reach on their own. The effect is on the state, not the tissue.

## What each is good for

**Choose massage when:** your shoulders are physically knotted, your back hurts from a long flight, you've been training, you want to be worked on and feel it.

**Choose Reiki when:** you're exhausted but can't nap, you sleep badly with no physical cause, you're anxious and don't know why, you've just moved and haven't landed, you're tense in a way massage helps for an afternoon and then it's back.

That last one is the tell. If massage keeps helping and the tension keeps coming back within a day, the tension isn't in the muscle. It's in the setting the nervous system is running at. That's Reiki's territory.

## Can you have both?

Yes, and for a lot of people on the Riviera the best week includes both. Massage first, Reiki the next day, is a good order: the body is already loosened, and the session goes deeper. Some hotels on the Croisette have excellent massage; I come to the room the following afternoon. Two different jobs, done properly.

## Where they overlap

Both produce relaxation. Both are better in a quiet room. Neither treats a medical condition — massage isn't physiotherapy, and Reiki is a complementary practice, not medicine. If you have a real injury, see a physio; if you have a real condition, see a doctor. Both of these practices sit alongside care, not in place of it.

## What people say afterwards

After massage: "my shoulders feel better." After Reiki: "I slept nine hours" or "I didn't realise how tense I was until it stopped." One client — long-standing tension in the back, neck and shoulders — had been getting massages every two weeks for a year. They helped, briefly. After a few Reiki sessions she said the ease of movement was coming back on its own between sessions, which hadn't happened with massage alone. I don't think Reiki did what massage does. I think it addressed the reason she needed massage every two weeks.

## Cost, for what it's worth

A good massage on the Riviera runs €100–€200 an hour. A Reiki session with me is €180 for 45 minutes, at your hotel or villa or my space in Cannes. Similar price, different job.

## FAQ

**What's the difference between Reiki and massage?**
Massage applies pressure to muscle and tissue; Reiki is light hand contact, fully clothed, that works on the nervous system's state. One loosens the body, the other settles the system running it.

**Is Reiki better than massage?**
Neither is better; they do different things. Massage for physical tightness, Reiki for a state that won't switch off. If massage helps but the tension keeps returning, that's a sign Reiki is the missing piece.

**Can you have Reiki and massage in the same week?**
Yes. Massage first, Reiki the next day works well — the body is already loosened and the session goes deeper.

## If you're not sure which you need

Message me on WhatsApp and describe the tension in one sentence. I'll tell you honestly whether it sounds like a massage problem or a nervous-system one — and if it's massage, I'll say so.

title: Reiki for Headaches and Migraines: What People Report
meta_title: Reiki for Headaches and Migraines: What People Report
meta_description: Reiki for headaches and migraines — what people report, why tension headaches respond, and where it sits alongside your doctor. Cannes.
body:
Reiki doesn't treat headaches or migraines, and I'd be careful of anyone who says it does. What it does — and what people consistently report — is reduce the tension that a lot of headaches ride on. The jaw that's been clenched all day, the shoulders that have crept up to the ears, the neck holding a head that's been looking at a screen since seven. When that lets go for 45 minutes, the headache that was building often doesn't arrive, and the ones that do are described as shorter and softer.

That's the honest scope. It's narrower than some practitioners claim and wider than most doctors expect, and it's what I've seen in Cannes for long enough to say it plainly.

## The headaches that respond

Tension-type headaches — the band across the forehead, the ache at the base of the skull, the one that starts in the neck and climbs. These are muscular and nervous-system headaches, and a session that gets the whole system to stand down tends to take them with it.

Stress headaches, the Friday ones, the after-the-difficult-call ones. Same category.

Migraines are different. Reiki doesn't stop a migraine. What some migraine sufferers tell me is that regular sessions seem to lengthen the gaps between them, and that a session during the prodrome — the hours before, when you know one is coming — sometimes softens what follows. I report that as what I hear, not as a promise. Migraines need a doctor, and I'll say that before we book.

## Why the neck and jaw matter

Most people who come to me for headaches don't realise where they're holding. I'll rest a hand on the jaw and feel it release five minutes later, and they'll say they didn't know it was clenched. Same with the shoulders. The headache is the last link in a chain that starts lower, and a session works the whole chain without anyone having to think about it.

## What one client noticed

A woman who'd had headaches for years — the tension kind, most weeks — came to me for something else entirely, and mentioned the headaches almost as an aside. After three sessions she said she'd realised she hadn't had one in a fortnight. She hadn't done anything else differently. I don't take credit for the headaches stopping; I think her shoulders came down and the headaches lost their starting point.

## What a session for headaches looks like

The same as any session — 45 minutes, fully clothed, hands resting lightly on or above the body from the head down — but I stay longer at the head, the jaw, the neck and the shoulders. If you have a headache during the session, it often eases as the tension does. If you're headache-free, the session works on the ground the next one would grow in.

One session tells you whether your headaches are the kind that respond. Four over a month — The Renewal — is where people say the frequency changes.

## Where the doctor comes in

New headaches, headaches that wake you, headaches with vision changes, the worst headache of your life: doctor, today, not Reiki. Migraines that are new or changing: neurologist. Anything you're taking medication for: keep taking it. This is a complementary practice; it sits alongside that care and doesn't replace a single tablet of it.

## What to track

If you're deciding whether this is working, don't track "did I have a headache." Track three things over a month: how many days had one, how long each lasted, and whether you reached for painkillers less. Those are the markers people report shifting, and they shift unevenly — a good fortnight, then a bad week, then better. The trend matters, not the day.

## FAQ

**Can Reiki help with headaches?**
It helps with the tension a lot of headaches ride on — jaw, neck, shoulders. People report tension headaches arriving less often and passing faster. It isn't a treatment and doesn't replace a doctor.

**Does Reiki work for migraines?**
It doesn't stop a migraine. Some people report longer gaps between them with regular sessions, and a softer episode after a session in the hours before one. Migraines need a doctor first.

**How many Reiki sessions for headaches?**
One shows whether yours are the responsive kind. Four over a month is where people typically notice frequency changing.

## If your headaches are the tension kind

Message me on WhatsApp and tell me where they start — forehead, neck, behind the eyes. I'll tell you whether it sounds like something a session addresses. The Renewal is four sessions, €640; a single is €180.

title: Your First Reiki Session: What to Expect (and What Not To)

meta_description: Your first Reiki session, step by step — from the WhatsApp message to the day after. What happens, what doesn't, and what to wear. Cannes and the Riviera.
keyword: first reiki session what to expect
body:
Your first Reiki session goes like this: a short exchange on WhatsApp to agree time and place; a 45-minute session lying down, fully clothed, with light hand contact and no conversation; a few minutes to come back; and a night's sleep that most people describe as different. There's no form to fill in, nothing to bring, nothing to believe, and nothing that happens to you that you haven't agreed to.

Here's the whole thing in order, so there are no surprises.

## Before: the WhatsApp exchange

You message me. I ask three things: what's brought you here in a sentence, where you'd like the session — your home, villa, hotel, or my space in Cannes — and when. I'll also ask if there's anything medical I should know about, because if there is, I'll tell you to see a doctor first. That's it. No questionnaire, no history. Five minutes.

## What to wear

Whatever you're wearing. Fully clothed, throughout. Comfortable is better than smart — you'll be lying down for 45 minutes — but I've worked on people in suits between meetings and it was fine. Take off shoes, a belt if it's tight, a watch if it bothers you. Nothing else.

## Arriving

If I'm coming to you, I'll arrive on time and quietly, with nothing but myself. If you're coming to me, the space is a calm room in Cannes; you'll be offered water and shown where to lie. There are no candles you didn't ask for. No music unless you want it. I'll ask how you slept and whether anything hurts, and then we begin.

## The session

You lie on your back. I start at the head and work down to the feet, hands resting lightly on or just above the body, moving through a set sequence. I don't talk. You don't have to. There's nothing to do — not to relax, not to breathe in any particular way, not to think of anything. Most people are still thinking for the first five or ten minutes and then, without deciding to, stop. Some fall asleep. Some feel warmth, or heaviness, or a strange lightness. Some feel nothing much and that's fine too.

Forty-five minutes. It usually feels shorter.

## Coming back

I finish at the feet and step back. I'll leave you lying for a minute before I say anything, because coming up fast from that depth is unpleasant. Then you sit up slowly. You'll probably be thirsty and a bit disoriented in a pleasant way. If you want to tell me what you noticed, I'll listen. If you don't, we don't. I'll never ask you to interpret or report an experience you didn't have.

## After

Drink water. Don't plan anything demanding for the next hour if you can help it. Most people sleep well that night — that's the most common first change, and the one worth paying attention to. Some feel emotional that evening; it passes. Some feel very little until the next morning, and then notice they're calmer than they've been in a while.

Elena, a client, spent the day before her first session in bed with no energy at all. She wrote the next day that she felt, in her word, recharged. That's not the typical first session — most are quieter — but it's what a first one can be.

## What doesn't happen

I don't diagnose. I don't tell you what's "blocked". I don't suggest a package before you've had a session. I don't ask you to stop seeing your doctor — this is a complementary practice, and it works alongside medical care, not instead. And I don't discuss who I see, so nothing about your session goes anywhere.

## If you need to leave early

Occasionally someone has to. A call, a child, a car. Tell me at the start and I'll shape the session to the time we have — thirty minutes is still worth doing. What I'd rather avoid is a phone ringing halfway through; it undoes more than it seems. Phone in another room, or with whoever's waiting for you.

## FAQ

**What should I wear to a Reiki session?**
Whatever you're comfortable lying down in. You stay fully clothed throughout; only shoes come off.

**What happens in a first Reiki session?**
Forty-five minutes lying on your back with light hand contact from head to feet, no conversation, nothing to do. Most people go into deep rest within ten minutes.

**How will I feel after my first Reiki session?**
Usually thirsty, calm and a little disoriented for an hour, then sleep that night that's noticeably deeper. Some feel emotional for an evening; it passes.

## If you'd like to book your first

Message me on WhatsApp with where you are and when suits. A single session is €180, at your home, hotel or my space in Cannes. If it's your first days here, ask about the Arrival Reset.

title: Reiki for Period Pain and Cycle Discomfort

meta_description: Reiki for period pain — what one client noticed right after a session, why tension and cramping travel together, alongside your gynaecologist.
body:
A client came to me for something else — stress, mostly — and mentioned, almost as a footnote, that her period pain had become noticeably worse since her move to the Riviera. Sharp, the first two days, enough to cancel things. After one session, timed a day before her cycle, she messaged to say the discomfort that month had been noticeably easier. Right after the session, in her words.

I'm starting with the case because it's the honest shape of what I can tell you about Reiki for period pain: it's what one woman noticed, it happened once and then again the next month, and I don't fully know why. What I can offer is the pattern I think is underneath it, and where this sits next to a gynaecologist — which is alongside, never instead.

## Why tension and cramping travel together

Menstrual pain is partly muscular — the uterus contracting — and partly everything around it: a pelvis and lower back held tight, a stomach braced against the pain before it arrives, a nervous system on alert because the last few cycles were bad. That bracing doesn't cause the pain, but it amplifies it, and it makes the body hold the pain longer than it needs to.

A session doesn't touch the uterus. What it does is get the whole system to stand down — pelvis, lower back, abdomen, the breath — for 45 minutes. Women describe the lower body going heavy and warm in a way it hasn't in years. What they report afterwards is that the cramping, when it comes, has less to grip.

## When to time it

The two or three days before the cycle, if you can. A session on the first day of pain also helps in the moment — the discomfort often eases during and for hours after — but the pre-cycle session seems to change more. If you're tracking, we book against the tracking.

## What I hear most

"I didn't realise I was holding my stomach in all the time." "The lower back let go and I didn't know it was tight." "This month I didn't cancel."

Those are the sentences. I don't hear "it's gone." I hear "it's easier" and "it's shorter," and from a couple of women, "it's like it used to be before things got bad."

## What a session looks like

The same as any session — lying down, fully clothed, hands resting lightly on or above the body, head to feet — with more time at the lower back, the abdomen and the hips. If you're in pain during, tell me and I'll stay where it helps. It's 45 minutes. Nothing is applied or pressed.

## Where the doctor is

Pain that's new, getting worse, or stopping your life: gynaecologist. Heavy bleeding, pain between cycles, anything you've been told to watch: gynaecologist. If you have a diagnosis — endometriosis, fibroids, cysts — keep every appointment and every treatment; some of the women I work with live with exactly these and use sessions for the tension and the rest alongside their care. That's the right order. Reiki is complementary. It's the calm around the medicine, not a replacement for it.

## What I'm not claiming

That Reiki changes hormones, shortens cycles, or does anything to the uterus. I have no basis to say any of that and I won't. What I'm describing is a body that stopped bracing for 45 minutes and reported, that month, that the pain had less to hold on to. Whether that's the whole explanation or part of one, I don't know. One woman's month is one woman's month — I'd want you to try it and judge by yours.

## FAQ

**Can Reiki help with period pain?**
It helps with the tension and bracing that amplify cramping. One client reported noticeably easier discomfort right after a session timed before her cycle. It's not a treatment, and it works alongside your gynaecologist.

**When is the best time for Reiki during your cycle?**
Two or three days before, if you're tracking. A session on the first day of pain also eases things in the moment.

**Is Reiki safe if I have endometriosis or fibroids?**
Yes — it's light hand contact with nothing applied. Keep every medical appointment; sessions sit alongside that care for the tension and rest, never instead.

## If your cycle has become something you dread

Message me on WhatsApp with roughly where you are in your cycle and I'll suggest timing. A single session is €180, at your home or my space in Cannes.

## Why massage helps for a day

If your shoulders are tight because of a specific strain — you lifted something, you slept wrong — massage is the right answer and I'll tell you so. But if they're tight because they've been tight for two years, because the jaw is clenched by default, because you sit at a screen braced for the next message, then the tightness isn't in the muscle. It's an instruction the nervous system keeps sending: *hold.* Massage loosens the muscle; the instruction resumes by the next morning.

A Reiki session works on the instruction. For 45 minutes the whole system gets every signal that it can stop holding — stillness, warmth, nothing asked — and at some point, usually without you noticing, it does. The shoulders drop. The jaw softens. The lower back, which you didn't know was involved, goes heavy.

A woman running a business between Antibes and London had carried tension in the back, neck and shoulders for as long as she could remember, and had been getting massage every couple of weeks to manage it. title: Distance Reiki for Travellers: Sessions Between Nice and London
