title: From "I Just Want to Lie Down" to Wanting to Create — a Story About Apathy and No Energy
meta_title: From "I Just Want to Lie Down" to Wanting to Create
meta_description: A client story about apathy and no energy — from wanting only to lie down to wanting to cook, then to build. What shifted over a month of Reiki.
body:
"I just want to lie down all day." That was the sentence she arrived with. Not ill — she'd checked, blood tests were fine. Not depressed, she thought, though she'd wondered. Just empty. Nothing was wrong and nothing was wanted. She'd moved to the coast eighteen months earlier, the move had gone well, and somewhere along the way she'd run out.

I'm telling this story because "no energy" and "apathy" are the words people search when they're in this state, and most of what they find is either a checklist of medical causes or a motivational post. This is neither. It's what happened over a month, in the order it happened, with the parts I don't understand left in.

## What apathy is, from where I sit

Not laziness. Not sadness exactly. It's the state where the reserve that makes wanting possible has been drawn down to nothing. You can still do things — she was running a household, working part-time — but nothing pulls. The pulling has stopped. Getting up is possible; wanting to is not.

It often follows a long stretch of alert. The nervous system runs high for months — a move, a business, a hard year — and then, when the emergency is over, it doesn't come down to rest. It comes down to flat. The alert has used up whatever fuels wanting, and flat is what's left.

## Session one

She lay down at home, sceptical and tired, and was asleep within five minutes. I worked the full sequence; she didn't stir. Afterwards she said she'd expected to feel something and had felt nothing, except that she'd slept — which she said she hadn't done properly in months, in the middle of the day, without guilt.

That night she slept nine hours.

## Session two, a week later

She mentioned, almost embarrassed, that she'd found herself wanting to cook. Not for anyone; just wanting to. She hadn't cooked for pleasure in a year. She didn't connect it to the session and I didn't push the connection. But wanting had appeared, small, in a place that had been flat.

## Session three

Quieter. She was awake through most of it, and said afterwards that she'd noticed her body for the first time in a long time — that it had weight and warmth and was hers. She'd started walking in the mornings along the Cap d'Antibes path. Not for exercise. Because she wanted to.

## Session four

She talked about a project. Something she'd shelved when the move happened and hadn't thought about since. She wasn't sure she'd do it. She was sure she wanted to. That was the difference between session one and session four: wanting.

## What I think happened

The nervous system had been flat because it had been alert for too long and then had nowhere to land. Four experiences of deep rest — real rest, with nothing asked — gave it somewhere. Once the system was resting instead of flat, the reserve started to refill, and wanting came back the way appetite comes back after illness: small, then real.

I don't take credit for the project or the cooking or the walks. The wanting was hers. What the sessions did, I think, was stop maintaining the emptiness so that it could.

## What I'd say to someone in that state

Get the blood tests. Rule out what a doctor can rule out — Reiki is complementary and this is exactly the situation where a doctor should be involved first. Then, if the answer is "nothing's wrong and I'm still empty," consider that the emptiness might be a system that needs rest it can't give itself. Four sessions over a month is what I'd suggest. And the first sign to watch for isn't energy. It's wanting.

## FAQ

**What causes having no energy when nothing is medically wrong?**
Often a nervous system that ran on alert for months and came down to flat rather than rest. The reserve that makes wanting possible is empty. It refills with real rest, which the body can't always provide itself.

**Can Reiki help with apathy?**
It gives the system repeated deep rest with nothing asked. In this client's case, wanting came back over four sessions — cooking first, then walking, then a project. Always after a doctor has ruled out medical causes.

**How long does it take to get energy back?**
In this story, four weeks from "I just want to lie down" to wanting to build something. Every person is different, and the first sign is small.

## If nothing pulls anymore

Get the tests first. Then message me on WhatsApp. The Renewal is four sessions over a month, €640, at your home. The first thing to watch for is wanting.

title: Clarity in a Difficult Relationship: What Reiki Did (and Didn't) Do
meta_title: Clarity in a Difficult Relationship: What Reiki Did
meta_description: A client stuck for months on a relationship found clarity after one Reiki session — not an answer from me, the noise clearing. What happened.
body:
She'd talked about it for months — to friends, to a therapist, to herself at 3 am. Whether to stay, whether to go, whether the thing she was feeling was a reason or an excuse. She came to me not to talk about it. She was tired of talking about it. She wanted, in her words, to stop going in circles.

I want to be careful here, because "Reiki for relationship clarity" could sound like I claim to fix relationships, and I don't. What follows is one session, one person, and my honest reading of what shifted and what didn't.

## Why circles

A hard decision about a person keeps the nervous system in alert, because the person is always there — in the house, in the phone, in the next conversation. Alert narrows thinking to threat logic: what could go wrong, what to defend. In that state the mind runs the same three arguments on a loop and never gets to the fourth thing, the one that's actually true. That's the circle. It's not indecision. It's a body that won't stand down long enough for the mind to see past the fear.

Talking, however good, can keep the circle going. Every conversation re-alerts the system to the problem.

## The session

At her home, 45 minutes, fully clothed. I didn't ask about the relationship and she didn't tell me. Hands resting lightly on the body — I stayed longer at the chest, where she was holding, and at the head. She was awake throughout, she said, but somewhere in the middle the arguing in her head simply stopped. Not resolved. Stopped. She described it as the first silence in months.

Afterwards she was quiet for a while, and then said she knew what to do next. It wasn't the dramatic option she'd been rehearsing. It was smaller, and it was hers.

## What I think happened

Nothing about the relationship changed in 45 minutes. What changed was the state she was looking at it from. When the body stood down, the threat logic switched off, and the thing she'd been unable to see past the fear became visible. She'd known it, I think, the whole time. The noise was in the way.

## What Reiki didn't do

Give her the answer. I didn't know what it was and still don't. Fix the relationship — that's her work and her partner's, not mine. Replace the therapist — she went back, and the session gave her something to bring. Reiki is complementary. If a relationship situation involves fear for your safety, or the distress has become something a doctor should see, that comes first, and I'll say so.

## For anyone in the circle

If you've been going round for months, a session isn't a way to decide. It's a way to stop long enough that the decision you've already made can surface. One is usually enough for that. Some people come back monthly while they act on it; that's a different conversation.

I also work with cutting energetic cords — a practice for the pull that stays after a relationship has changed — but that's for after clarity, not before it. There's a separate piece on what it is and isn't.

## Why I don't ask

People sometimes find it strange that I don't want to know. The reason is simple: if I know, I have an opinion, and an opinion in the room is one more voice in a head that's already full of them. The session works because nothing is being added. You lie down with the whole thing exactly as tangled as it is, and for 45 minutes no one — including me — is trying to untangle it. That's the condition in which people find their own thread.

## FAQ

**Can Reiki help with relationship decisions?**
It doesn't give answers. It gets the nervous system out of the alert state that keeps a decision circling, so what you already know can surface. One client stuck for months found her next step in one session.

**Should I talk about my relationship during a Reiki session?**
Only if you want to. I don't ask. The session works on the body's side; the talking is for a therapist or a friend.

**Is Reiki a substitute for couples therapy?**
No. It's complementary — it can make the person calmer and clearer going into therapy, and that's all it claims.

## If you're going in circles

One session, €180, at your home or my space in Cannes. Message me on WhatsApp. You don't have to tell me what it's about.

title: Can't Sleep After a Long Flight? A 48-Hour Plan
meta_title: Can't Sleep After a Long Flight? A 48-Hour Plan
meta_description: Can't sleep after a long flight? A 48-hour plan for the Riviera — light, meals, the nap rule, and one session that settles the nervous system.
body:
You landed exhausted and now, at 2 am in a hotel in Cannes, you're wide awake. This is the most common thing that happens after a long flight, and it's not insomnia — it's a body clock that's in the wrong time zone plus a nervous system that hasn't come down from eleven hours in a seat. Both are fixable in 48 hours if you do a few specific things in a specific order.

Here's the plan. It's short because you're tired.

## Tonight (whatever hour it is)

**Don't fight it.** Lying in the dark being furious about being awake keeps the alert system on. Get up, dim light, something boring — not a screen, or a screen on its lowest setting with the blue filter on. Go back when your eyes are heavy, not when you think you should.

**Cool the room.** Shutters down, air on. The body sleeps better a degree cooler.

**No alcohol to "help".** It knocks you out and wakes you at 4.

## Day one

**Morning light, outside.** Twenty minutes minimum, before 10 am. The Croisette, the port, anywhere with sky. This is the single strongest signal to the body clock, and most people skip it because they're tired.

**Breakfast at breakfast time**, even if you're not hungry. Meals are the second clock.

**The nap rule:** twenty minutes, before 3 pm, with an alarm. Two hours at 4 pm and tonight is gone.

**Move gently.** A walk to the Îles de Lérins ferry and back. Not a run.

**A session in the afternoon or evening.** This is the part I'd add to any jet-lag plan, and the reason the Arrival Reset exists. Forty-five minutes in your hotel room, lying down, fully clothed. It settles the nervous system — the part that's still braced from the flight and won't let the rest signals land. Most people sleep properly that night, which is what turns a three-day adjustment into one.

## Night one

Bed at local bedtime, not before. Same cool dark room. If you did the light, the meals and the session, this is usually the night it works.

## Day two

Repeat the light and the meals. Skip the nap if you can. Notice that you're mostly here. By the evening of day two, most people are through the worst of it.

## Why the session matters

A flight is a long stretch of low-level alert — noise, dry air, no sleep, a body held still. The tiredness you feel on arrival is real, but so is a background hum that won't turn down: heart a little fast, mind a little loud. Until that stands down, you can do everything right and still be awake at 3 am. A session gives the body a strong, direct signal that it can stop. There's a longer explanation in [how to deal with jet lag after travel](/journal/how-to-deal-with-jet-lag-after-travel/); this is the version for tonight.

If you have a condition that travel affects, or sleeplessness that predates the flight, that's a doctor's conversation. Reiki is complementary and this plan is for the ordinary body-clock kind.

## If you're arriving from the east or the west

From New York, Dubai or Asia, the direction matters slightly. Coming from the west — the Americas — you're behind local time; afternoon light and staying up until a normal bedtime pull you forward. Coming from the east — the Gulf, Asia — you're ahead; morning light and an earlier night help. The session works the same from either direction. It's the part of the plan that doesn't care which way you flew.

## FAQ

**Why can't I sleep after a long flight even though I'm exhausted?**
Body clock in the wrong zone plus a nervous system still in alert from the flight. Tired and wired at the same time. Light, meals at local times and one real rest fix it in about 48 hours.

**Should I nap after a long-haul flight?**
Twenty minutes before 3 pm, with an alarm. Anything longer costs you the night.

**What's the fastest way to reset after flying to the Riviera?**
Morning light outside, meals at local times, no long nap, and a session in the first 48 hours to settle the nervous system. Most people sleep properly the first night after that.

## If you're reading this at 2 am

Message me on WhatsApp — I'll see it in the morning and can often come the same day. The Arrival Reset is €180, in your hotel or villa, and the earlier in the 48 hours we do it, the more of your week you get back.

title: Does Distance Reiki Really Work? What I Can and Can't Tell You
meta_title: Does Distance Reiki Really Work? Honest Answer
meta_description: Does distance Reiki really work? What the tradition says, what clients report, what I can't explain, and how to test it yourself.
body:
Does distance Reiki work? Here's the most honest answer I can give: the people who receive it report the same things as people who receive it in person — deep rest, warmth or pressure where my hands are, better sleep that night — and they report it consistently, from London and Dubai and a plane over the Alps. That's what I know. What I don't know is the mechanism, and I'd rather say that plainly than build you a theory you'd have to accept before booking.

This piece is for the person who wants to try it and needs to know what they're being asked to believe. The answer is: nothing. Here's why.

## What the tradition says

Distance practice is part of second-degree Usui Reiki and has been since the 1920s. One of the three second-degree symbols exists specifically for it. Practitioners have given sessions to people in other cities for a century — long before anyone did anything online. So this isn't a pandemic workaround. It's a defined practice with a defined place in the training I did.

That tells you it's real in the tradition's terms. It doesn't tell you it works. For that, you need what people report.

## What people report

I'll be specific, because vague is useless.

- **Sensation where my hands are.** The most common thing. Warmth, pressure, sometimes a pull, in the exact place I'm working on the proxy at that moment — without knowing the sequence. I've had people message me during a session to say "are you at my stomach?" and I was.
- **The drop.** Around minute ten, same as in person. Thinking slows, body goes heavy, time stops behaving.
- **Sleep.** That night. Reported by nearly everyone.
- **Nothing during, something after.** A quiet session and then a different next day.

People who've had both formats say the distance version is quieter — no one in the room, no journey — and that the effect is the same.

## What I can explain

The attention. For 45 minutes one person is holding calm, unhurried, undivided attention on you, and you know it. You've set the time, you've lain down, you're expecting it. The body responds to being attended to; the nervous system reads it as safety. That alone would account for the drop and the sleep, and it requires no belief.

## What I can't explain

The sensation in the right place. I don't know why people feel my hands where they are. I've stopped pretending to, and I've stopped being surprised by it.

## How to test it

Book one. Lie down at the agreed time in a quiet room. Don't try to feel anything — think about work if you like. Track two things afterwards: how you slept, and how easily you got irritated the next day. Judge by that, not by the hour. If it did nothing, you've had a 45-minute rest and you're €180 down. If it did something, you'll know.

Reiki is complementary in any form. A distance session doesn't replace a doctor for anything that needs one, and I'll say so if I hear it.

## A note on expectation

People sometimes worry that distance sessions "work" because they expect them to — that it's just expectation. Maybe part of it is. I'd point out that expectation doesn't usually produce a sensation of warmth at the stomach at the exact minute my hands are there, and that plenty of people who booked out of curiosity, expecting nothing, report the same. But I'm not going to argue you out of the placebo question. I'd rather you tested it and decided.

## FAQ

**Does distance Reiki really work?**
People report the same things as in-person sessions — warmth where my hands are, deep rest, better sleep — consistently and from anywhere. I can explain part of it (attention) and not the rest. The way to know is to try one.

**Is distance Reiki as effective as in-person?**
Clients who've done both say the effect is the same and the distance version is quieter. Some prefer it.

**How do I know a distance session actually happened?**
I message you when it's done, and most people can tell — sensation during, the drop, sleep after. Some people message me mid-session to ask where I am on the body, and they're right.

## If you'd like to test it

A distance session is €180. Message me on WhatsApp with your time zone and a quiet window. Bring your scepticism. It doesn't get in the way.

## The shape of it

Executive burnout rarely looks like collapse. It looks like a person who's still functional and hollow. Sleep is short and light. Weekends don't restore. Decisions that used to be easy feel heavy. Irritation at small things, flatness at good news. A body that hurts — jaw, shoulders, stomach — in ways scans don't explain. And, in the ones who've moved here to recover, a particular kind of guilt: I have everything I wanted and I'm not better.

## Why it doesn't lift on its own

The nervous system doesn't have a "retired" setting. It has alert and rest, and for someone who's run a company through crises, alert has been the default for so long that rest has become something they fall into from exhaustion rather than something they can enter. Because burnout is a nervous-system setting, not a location. A view doesn't give the body the repeated experience of rest it needs to unlearn years of alert.

title: Reiki for Stress Relief: What It Does That a Glass of Rosé Doesn't

meta_description: Reiki for stress relief — the difference between taking the edge off and changing the setting, why rosé wears off by morning, what a session does instead.
body:
A glass of rosé on the terrace takes the edge off. So does a run, a bath, a good dinner, an hour of something on Netflix. All of these work — for the evening. By morning the setting is back where it was: shoulders up, breath short, mind already at the desk. That's the difference between stress relief and stress change. Relief is turning the volume down for a few hours. Change is the nervous system learning a different default.

Reiki for stress relief does the second thing, and the reason is worth understanding, because it's also the reason a session feels like so little while it's happening.

## Relief versus setting

Stress is a setting, not an event. The body decides how alert to be based on the signals it's been getting — demand, noise, uncertainty, the phone — and it holds that setting until the signals change. A glass of wine changes the signal for an evening. Sleep partially resets it. But if the day starts with the same demands, the setting is back by 8 am.

Changing the setting needs the body to have repeated experiences of the opposite: stillness, warmth, nothing needed, long enough to believe it. That's not something most people give themselves. Even a holiday on the Riviera has demand in it — where to eat, who to meet, the emails that came in.

## What a session does instead

Forty-five minutes lying down, fully clothed, at your home or my space in Cannes. Hands resting lightly on the body in a set sequence. No conversation. No instruction to relax, breathe correctly or think of nothing — those are demands too. The body is simply given, for 45 minutes, every signal that it can stand down, and somewhere around minute ten it does. The jaw lets go. The shoulders drop. The breath goes all the way down.

That's stress relief while it's happening. What makes it stress change is doing it again. By the third or fourth session, the body starts to expect the drop, and the drop starts to be available on Tuesday afternoon without a session. That's The Renewal — four over a month.

## What people say

"I didn't know I was that tense until it stopped." "I slept through for the first time in weeks." "I noticed on Thursday that my shoulders were down on their own." Not "I feel relaxed" — that's the rosé sentence. These are the setting-change sentences.

One client came for what she called general stress and mentioned, later, that the headaches she'd had most weeks for years had stopped somewhere around the third session. She hadn't come for the headaches. The setting changed and they lost their starting point.

## Rosé is still fine

I'm not against the terrace. I'm saying it does a different job. If you want an evening off, have the glass. If you want to stop needing the evening off, that's a different tool.

Stress that has become something a doctor should see — chest tightness, panic, sleep that's gone entirely — is a medical conversation first. Reiki is complementary; it sits alongside that care, not instead.

## The setting on a Tuesday afternoon

The test of whether stress has actually changed isn't how you feel after a session. It's a random Tuesday afternoon, three weeks in, when you notice — without a session, without wine, without a holiday — that your shoulders are down and you've been sitting with a coffee for twenty minutes without reaching for the phone. Clients describe that moment with a kind of surprise, as if they'd caught themselves resting. That's the setting having changed. Everything before it was relief.

## FAQ

**Does Reiki help with stress?**
Yes, and differently from most things: it changes the nervous system's setting rather than taking the edge off for an evening. People report the effect lasting between sessions, not just during.

**How is Reiki different from just relaxing?**
Relaxing is something you do; a session is something you receive with nothing asked. The body responds to the absence of demand, which most relaxation still contains.

**How many sessions for stress?**
One shows you what the drop feels like. Four over a month is where the setting starts to change on its own.

Message me on WhatsApp. One session, €180, or The Renewal, four for €640, at your home or my space in Cannes. Keep the rosé.

title: Ancestral Patterns: What You Carry From Your Family Line

body:
My grandfather worked with energy long before the word Reiki reached where he lived. I didn't learn from him directly — I was too young — but I grew up in a house where it was normal for someone to put their hands on a person who hurt, and where it was normal for that to help. When I found Reiki decades later, it felt less like learning something new than being handed back something I already carried. That's my ancestral pattern, and it's a fortunate one.

Not everyone's is. This piece is about what a family line passes down beyond eye colour, why it surfaces when you move abroad, and how I work with it — with the honest caveat that this is the least measurable thing I do, and I'll tell you where knowledge ends and practice begins.

## What gets passed down

Some of it is documented. Children of people who lived through war, famine or displacement carry patterns of alert — vigilance, scarcity thinking, a nervous system tuned to threat — that show up two or three generations later without anyone being told the story. Researchers call this intergenerational trauma; families call it "that's just how we are."

Some of it is simpler. The way your mother braced when the phone rang. The way your father never sat down. The rule, never spoken, that rest is earned and you haven't earned it. You absorbed these before you could speak, and your body runs them as defaults.

## Why it surfaces abroad

Moving countries strips away the context that made the patterns invisible. At home everyone around you had the same defaults, so they looked like reality. Here in Cannes, surrounded by people whose families sat down, whose phones ringing didn't mean bad news, the pattern becomes visible — as a difference. People describe it as suddenly seeing their own reflexes from outside. Often it's uncomfortable. Sometimes it's the first time they can be worked with.

## How I work with it

I don't do ceremony. I don't call on ancestors or tell you what your great-grandmother went through. What I do is sessions — 45 minutes, lying down, hands resting lightly on the body — with attention on the places where the pattern lives physically: the braced chest, the held breath, the shoulders that never came down because nobody's in that line ever did.

The second-degree symbol for the emotional and mental layer, Sei He Ki, is what I bring to this. In the tradition it's used for exactly this kind of thing — what's carried rather than what's strained. The body, over sessions, gets a repeated experience of the opposite of the pattern: rest without earning it, safety without a phone call. Slowly, it learns the difference between the inherited default and the actual present.

## What changes, and what doesn't

The pattern doesn't disappear. What people describe is noticing it sooner and being less run by it — the flinch when the phone rings, and then, a beat later, "oh, that's my mother's." That beat is the change. It's the space where a choice becomes possible.

This is slow work. I suggest The Immersion — eight sessions over two to three months — because a pattern older than you needs a container longer than a month. And I won't take anyone into it who hasn't had a single session first; you should know what my hands feel like before you commit to something this long.

## Honesty about what this is

It's practice, not science. I can tell you what I see and what people report. I can't show you a mechanism. If what you're carrying includes trauma that needs a therapist, or symptoms a doctor should see, that comes first — Reiki is complementary, alongside that work, never instead. What I offer is a body-level companion to it.

## FAQ

**What are ancestral patterns?**
Defaults you absorbed from your family line before you could choose — vigilance, scarcity, never resting — some documented as intergenerational trauma, some simply the way your parents held themselves.

**Why do family patterns show up more after moving abroad?**
Because the context that made them invisible is gone. Surrounded by people with different defaults, you see your own from outside for the first time.

**How does Reiki work with ancestral patterns?**
Through repeated sessions that give the body the opposite experience — rest without earning it — with attention on where the pattern lives physically. It's practice, not science, and it sits alongside therapy where that's needed.

title: Cutting Energetic Cords: An Honest Explanation

Cutting energetic cords is a practice for the pull that stays after something has ended. A relationship is over and you still feel it in the chest at 3 pm. I'll explain what it is, what it isn't, and when I do it — which is after clarity, not before, for reasons I'll get to.

## What the pull is

In plain terms: the nervous system keeps a channel open to people and situations it's spent a long time attending to. That's not mystical; it's what attention does. You spent years reading a partner's mood before they spoke, and the reading doesn't stop because they left. You spent years bracing for a boss's email, and the bracing doesn't stop because you resigned. The channel is still open and something keeps flowing down it — a tug, a checking, a low hum of them.

The tradition calls that a cord. I find the word useful because it matches what people describe: something attached at the chest or the stomach, pulling.

## What the practice is

A session — 45 minutes, lying down, hands resting lightly on the body — with specific attention on where the pull is felt. Usually the chest or the solar plexus. I use the second-degree symbols, particularly Sei He Ki, which is for the emotional layer, and I work with the intention of releasing what's attached. There's no ceremony you have to take part in, nothing to say, no visualising a pair of scissors. You lie there. I work.

What people describe: a heaviness at the place of the pull, then a loosening, sometimes tears, and afterwards a quietness where the hum used to be. One woman described it as "the room they were standing in got emptier."

## What it isn't

It's not a way to end a relationship, or to get someone back, or to affect them in any way. It works on your side of the channel only. It's not a substitute for the grief or the anger that ending something involves — those still have to be felt. And it's not magic: if you go back to the person or the job the next day, the channel reopens.

## Why after clarity, not before

If you're still deciding — whether to stay, whether to go — cutting a cord is the wrong tool. You'd be releasing something you haven't finished with, and the body knows it. The practice works when the decision has been made and what remains is the residue. That's why I ask, before doing it, whether the thing is actually over. If it isn't, I suggest a regular session instead — for the clarity — and we come back to this.

## When it helps most

After a breakup or divorce, when the practical part is done and the pull isn't. After leaving a role that defined you. After a parent's death, when the reflexes they installed are still running. After a friendship that ended badly. After leaving a country — yes, the pull to a place is real too, and expats know it.

Reiki is complementary in all of this. Grief, loss and the end of things sometimes need a therapist, and this practice sits alongside that work, not in place of it.

## After

The days after a cord session are often quiet in a way people don't expect. The hum is gone and the space where it was is empty, and empty can feel like loss for a day or two before it feels like room. I mention this so it doesn't surprise you. Fill the space with something of your own — a walk, a plan, sleep — and not with the person or the job it used to be attached to.

## FAQ

**What is cutting energetic cords?**
A practice for releasing the pull that stays after a relationship, role or place has ended — treated as a physical attachment at the chest or stomach, worked with in a session on your side only.

**Does cord cutting affect the other person?**
No. It works on your side of the channel. It doesn't end anything, bring anyone back, or influence them.

**When should I do cord cutting?**
After the decision is made and only the residue remains. If you're still deciding, a regular session for clarity comes first.

## If something is over and still pulling

Message me on WhatsApp and tell me, in a line, what ended. One session, €180, at your home or my space in Cannes. If it isn't over yet, I'll say so, and we'll start with something else.

title: Reiki for a Baby Who's Teething and Can't Sleep
meta_title: Reiki for a Teething Baby Who Can't Sleep
meta_description: Reiki for a teething baby who won't sleep — a very short, gentle format with a parent present, what it can and can't do, paediatrician first.
body:
A teething baby who won't sleep is a household that isn't sleeping, and by night four nobody in it is thinking clearly. Reiki for a baby is the gentlest form of what I do: five to fifteen minutes, with you holding them or beside them, my hands resting lightly on their back or feet, nothing else. It doesn't stop teething. What it can do is help a small nervous system that's been in distress for days to settle enough to sleep — and it always sits alongside the paediatrician, never in place of one.

I'm writing this for the parent searching at 3 am. Here's what it is, what it isn't, and the honest order of things.

## First: the paediatrician

Teething causes discomfort, drooling, chewing, some fussiness. It does not cause high fever, diarrhoea, rash, or a baby who won't feed. If any of those are present, that's the doctor, today, and nothing else until they've been seen. I'll ask before I come. If the baby needs a doctor, I'll say so and I won't book.

## What teething does to a small system

Pain in a body that can't understand it. The baby is in low-level alert for days — can't settle, wakes at every shift, and the tiredness makes the pain feel worse. The parent is in alert too, which the baby reads instantly. A house in this state feeds itself.

## What a session is

Very short. Five to fifteen minutes; longer than that and a baby is done. You hold them, or they lie beside you. I sit close and rest my hands lightly on the back, or the feet, and keep them there — still, warm, unhurried. No pressure, nothing near the mouth. I don't say anything to the baby. To them it's a calm adult, close, still.

Most babies settle within a few minutes. Some fall asleep against you. Some just stop crying and look around. Any of these is the session.

## What one family saw

A child who'd been waking most nights for months — older than teething, but the same kind of unsettled — began, after a few bedtime sessions, to sleep through. The parent's message was one line. I don't know exactly what changed. I know the child's body had a few experiences of someone steady beside it with nothing asked, and I know a house where the baby sleeps is a different house within days.

## The parent, again

A parent on night four of no sleep has a nervous system in worse shape than the baby's, and the baby knows. Honestly, the most useful thing I can do in a house like this is a session for you while someone else holds the child — 45 minutes horizontal with nothing asked, which you haven't had since before the teeth. Then, if it still makes sense, the baby. Sometimes the baby settles when you do.

## What it isn't

A treatment for teething. A replacement for the doctor, teething gel, paracetamol when the paediatrician says so, or any of the ordinary things. Reiki is complementary — the calm around the care, never the care.

## What the session looks like from the doorway

A parent on the bed with the baby against their chest. Me sitting close, one hand on the baby's back, still. No one speaking. After a few minutes the baby's breathing lengthens; the parent's does too — they can't help it. Sometimes the baby sleeps. Sometimes the parent nearly does. Ten minutes and I'm gone. From the doorway it looks like nothing. That's what it's supposed to look like.

## FAQ

**Is Reiki safe for a teething baby?**
Yes. Light hands resting on back or feet with a parent present, nothing applied, nothing near the mouth. Always alongside the paediatrician — if there's fever, rash or feeding problems, doctor first.

**How long is a Reiki session for a baby?**
Five to fifteen minutes. Any longer and a baby is done. The short version is the right version.

**Can Reiki help a baby sleep through teething?**
It can help a distressed small nervous system settle enough to sleep. It doesn't stop teething. One family saw an unsettled child begin sleeping through after a few bedtime sessions.

## If your house hasn't slept

Message me on WhatsApp — tell me the baby's age and what the nights look like. I'll ask about the paediatrician first. Baby sessions are very short and priced accordingly; a session for you may be the one to start with.

title: How to Choose a Reiki Practitioner Abroad: 7 Questions to Ask
meta_title: How to Choose a Reiki Practitioner Abroad: 7 Questions
meta_description: How to choose a Reiki practitioner abroad — seven questions about lineage, level, language, format, discretion, price and the doctor rule.
keyword: how to choose a reiki practitioner
body:
Choosing a Reiki practitioner in your own country, you have context: reviews in your language, a friend who knows someone. Abroad, in English, on the Riviera, you mostly have the practitioner's word. So the question is what to ask, and what a good answer sounds like. Here are the seven I'd ask anyone — including me. I've put my answers beside them so you can compare.

## 1. Who trained you, and in what lineage?

A real practitioner has a named teacher and a line back to Mikao Usui. It should be on a diploma you can see. If someone can't or won't name their teacher, that's the answer.

*Mine: Olena Yushko, Usui Reiki Ryoho, lineage through Hayashi and Takata. Both diplomas on the homepage.*

## 2. What level, and when?

Level 1 is hands-on in person. Level 2 adds the symbols and distance practice. Master is the teaching degree. For a full session anywhere, you want Level 2. Ask when — someone who says "Master" but trained last month is telling you about a course, not a practice.

*Mine: Level 1 December 2025, Level 2 February 2026. I say so plainly. What I bring alongside it is a family line of healers, ten years of sitting with people professionally, and daily practice.*

## 3. Do you work in my language?

Not just "speak it." Work in it. A session has almost no talking, but the exchange before and after does, and if you're describing something delicate you want to do it in a language you think in.

*Mine: English, Russian, Ukrainian. Not French — I'll say so rather than pretend.*

## 4. Where do sessions happen?

A cabinet you travel to, or they come to you. On the Riviera, with villas in Mougins and hotels on the Croisette and yachts in the bay, coming to you is the difference between a session and an errand.

*Mine: your home, villa, hotel, yacht, or my space in Cannes. Travel within Cannes–Antibes–Nice included.*

## 5. How discreet are you?

Ask directly. Some practitioners post client stories, host groups, or work from busy studios. If discretion matters to you, ask what happens to your name.

*Mine: I don't discuss who I see. No posts, no groups, no waiting room. I arrive as a visitor.*

## 6. What does it cost, and what's included?

A clear price, what it includes, whether travel is extra, how packages work. Vagueness here usually means vagueness elsewhere.

*Mine: €180 for 45 minutes with travel on the central Riviera. Packages from €480. Card, transfer or cash. Free rescheduling with 24 hours' notice.*

## 7. Will you tell me to see a doctor?

The most important one. The right answer is "yes, when you should — and I'll ask." A practitioner who says Reiki treats things, cures things, or means you can stop treatment is the one to walk away from. Reiki is complementary. It sits alongside medical care, never instead.

*Mine: I ask about anything medical before we book, and if a doctor should come first, I say so. Every article on this site says the same.*

## What the good answers have in common

They're specific. Names, dates, prices, places. They don't oversell — a practitioner who promises you'll be transformed hasn't understood the practice. And they include a "no" somewhere: no, I don't speak French; no, I won't do this instead of your doctor; no, I won't suggest a package before a session. The nos are how you know the yeses are real.

## One more thing to notice

How they respond to your first message. Fast and specific — a time, a place, a price, a question about anything medical — is a practitioner who runs a practice. Vague, or a link to a booking page, or a package before you've asked, is a practitioner who runs a funnel. The first exchange tells you most of what you'll find out later.

## FAQ

**How do I know if a Reiki practitioner is legitimate?**
Ask for their teacher's name and lineage back to Usui, their level and when they trained. It should be on a diploma you can see. Then ask whether they'll tell you to see a doctor — the answer should be yes.

**What level should a Reiki practitioner have?**
Level 2 for full sessions and distance practice. Master is a teaching qualification and doesn't in itself mean a better practitioner.

**What should a Reiki session cost on the French Riviera?**
€30–€80 at a French cabinet; €150–€220 for English-speaking, in-home practitioners. Ask what's included — travel, discretion, language — before comparing numbers.

## If you'd like to ask me any of these

Message me on WhatsApp. I'll answer all seven, and I'd rather you asked the hard ones first.

title: Reiki for Founders Between Two Countries
meta_title: Reiki for Founders Living Between Two Countries
meta_description: Reiki for founders between Nice and London, Dubai or New York — a rhythm of in-person and distance sessions that holds when you're never in one place.
body:
Energy healing for founders who live between two countries starts from one fact: your body is never entirely in either. Monday in a London office, Thursday on a terrace in Villefranche, phone in the same time zone as whoever's awake. The Riviera is supposed to be the place you rest, and it isn't, because the nervous system doesn't know which country it's in and defaults to alert in both.

I work with a number of people in this position, and what I've found is that the usual advice — rest when you're here, work when you're there — doesn't hold, because the body doesn't switch by geography. What holds is a rhythm that goes with you.

## The problem with two places

Rest is cumulative. The body learns to stand down through repetition — the third session goes deeper than the first because the first two taught it something. If sessions only happen when you're on the coast, and you're on the coast one week in three, the body never gets past the beginning. Every session is partly a restart.

The other problem is arrival. Every time you land — Nice on Thursday, Heathrow on Monday — the system goes back to alert. Two arrivals a week is a nervous system that never lands anywhere.

## A rhythm that travels

Sessions in person when you're here — at the villa, at my space in Cannes, on the boat if that's where you are. Sessions at a distance when you're not — Wednesday evening in the London flat, a Sunday afternoon in Dubai, mid-flight if the timing works. The same 45 minutes, the same sequence, the same attention. The body doesn't distinguish the way you'd expect, and the rhythm holds.

One founder — a company in London, a house in Villefranche — did three sessions here over a fortnight, then two at a distance from Marylebone during a month away, then back here. He said afterwards the London ones were quieter, that the sleep was the same, and that for the first time he'd arrived at Nice on a Thursday without the usual three days of adjustment. The body had been landing all month.

## The arrivals

I'd suggest, if you fly between places often, a session on the day you land — either end. Not every time, but when the week ahead matters. An Arrival Reset in the Cannes hotel or a distance session in the London flat on the evening you get in: the body gets a signal that this place, too, is somewhere it can stand down. Over months, arrivals stop being the thing that resets you to alert.

## What this looks like as a package

The Renewal — four sessions over a month — works fine across two countries. Two here, two there, in whatever order the calendar gives. Distance sessions are the same price as in person, so the package doesn't change. Sessions don't have to be in the same country to count.

## What I won't pretend

That distance sessions replace being here. Some people prefer them; some find in-person deeper. That any of this fixes a schedule that's genuinely impossible — sometimes the honest answer is fewer flights. Or that Reiki replaces a doctor if the sleeplessness has become medical. It's complementary, alongside care, not instead.

## The phone

One thing I ask of founders specifically: the phone goes in another room, not on silent beside you. A phone within reach is a nervous system that hasn't fully agreed to stand down; the body knows it's there. For 45 minutes, across two countries, this is the one demand I make. Everyone resists it and nobody regrets it.

## FAQ

**How can I keep Reiki sessions going when I travel for work?**
Distance sessions — same 45 minutes, same sequence, from Cannes to wherever you are. The rhythm carries on; the body doesn't lose the thread between countries.

**Do distance and in-person sessions work together?**
Yes. A founder I work with did three here and two from London in one month and said the effect was the same. Packages count sessions in any country.

**Should I have a session when I land?**
When the week ahead matters, yes — either end. It teaches the body that both places are somewhere it can stand down, and arrivals stop resetting you to alert.

## If you're between two places

Message me on WhatsApp with your rough calendar for the month. I'll suggest a rhythm — here and there — and it'll be €180 a session either way.

title: What Reiki Is Not: Clearing Up Five Common Misunderstandings
meta_title: What Reiki Is Not: Five Misunderstandings Cleared Up
meta_description: What Reiki is not — not massage, not religion, not a diagnosis, not a substitute for a doctor, not magic. What it is, plainly, from Cannes.
body:
Reiki is a Japanese practice, developed by Mikao Usui in the 1920s, in which a trained practitioner rests their hands lightly on or just above a fully clothed body for around 45 minutes, in a set sequence, with the intention of supporting the body's own rest and settling. The word joins *rei* — universal, or spirit — and *ki* — life energy, the same concept as *qi*. That's what it is. What follows is what it isn't, because the misunderstandings stop more people booking than the practice ever could.

## It's not massage

Nothing is pressed, kneaded or moved. You stay dressed. Hands rest and stay. If you want muscle worked, book a massage — it's a different tool for a different job, and there's a piece on which you need. Reiki works on the nervous system's setting, not the tissue.

## It's not a religion

Usui was a Buddhist; the practice isn't Buddhist. There's no belief required, no deity involved, nothing to join. The five "just for today" principles that came with it — don't worry, don't anger, be grateful, work honestly, be kind — are about as religious as good manners. I've worked with Catholics, atheists, Muslims and people who'd never thought about it, and the session is the same for all of them.

## It's not a diagnosis

I don't tell you what's "blocked," which chakra is "closed," or what your body is "saying." I'm not qualified to and neither is anyone else in this practice. I rest my hands, I notice where you're holding, and that's the extent of what I know about you afterwards. Anyone who diagnoses in a Reiki session is doing something other than Reiki.

## It's not a substitute for a doctor

This is the one that matters. Reiki doesn't treat, cure or replace anything. It sits alongside medical care — for the rest, the settling, the state around a condition — and if you describe something that needs a doctor, I'll say so before we book. A practitioner who suggests otherwise has stepped outside the practice and should be left there. There's a longer piece on how Reiki and medical treatment work together.

## It's not magic

Nothing happens that the body isn't already capable of. Deep rest, warmth, sleep, the drop into stillness — these are things the nervous system does when it's given the right conditions for long enough. A session provides the conditions. Does something else happen too — the warmth people feel in places I'm not touching, the sensations in a distance session? I think so, and I can't prove it, and you don't need to believe it for the rest of it to work.

## What it is, then

An hour where nothing is asked of you and someone holds calm, steady attention on your body until it stands down. In a life where that never otherwise happens — and for most of the people I see in Cannes, it doesn't — that turns out to be quite a lot.

## It's not a one-size ritual

The sequence is set — head to feet, in order — but the session isn't. A founder braced at the jaw gets longer at the jaw. Someone grieving gets longer at the chest. A highly sensitive person gets a dimmer room and hands held above rather than on. The practice is the same; the attention goes where the person is. Anyone who does exactly the same thing to everyone is doing a routine, not a session.

## FAQ

**What is Reiki, simply?**
A Japanese practice where a trained practitioner rests hands lightly on or above your clothed body for about 45 minutes to support deep rest and settling. Developed by Mikao Usui in the 1920s.

**Is Reiki a religion?**
No. It requires no belief and has no deity. Its five principles are ethical, not religious, and the session is the same regardless of faith.

**Does Reiki replace medical treatment?**
Never. It's complementary — alongside your doctor for rest and settling, not instead of anything.

## If you'd like to see for yourself

One session, €180, at your home or my space in Cannes. Message me on WhatsApp. Bring your doubts; they don't get in the way.

title: The Nervous System Explained Simply — and Where Reiki Fits
meta_title: The Nervous System Explained Simply — Where Reiki Fits
meta_description: The nervous system explained simply — alert and rest, why modern life sticks on alert, what fight-or-flight is, and where a Reiki session fits.
body:
You have one nervous system with two main settings. One is for doing — alert, ready, fast. The other is for repairing — rest, digestion, sleep, recovery. The first is often called fight-or-flight, the second rest-and-digest. Both are necessary. The problem in most modern lives, and especially in the lives of people who've just moved countries or run companies, is that the first setting gets stuck on and the second never gets a proper turn.

That's the whole thing. Everything else is detail — but the detail helps, because once you understand what your body is doing, most of what I do in a session stops sounding mystical and starts sounding obvious.

## The two settings

**Alert** — the sympathetic branch. Heart faster, breath shorter and higher, muscles slightly tense, attention narrowed to threat, digestion paused. Useful for a real emergency and for effort. Designed to be temporary.

**Rest** — the parasympathetic branch. Heart slower, breath deep, muscles loose, digestion running, repair happening. This is where sleep, healing, and the feeling of being fine live. Designed to be the default.

The body switches between them based on signals — what it sees, hears, feels, and what's being asked of it. A phone buzzing is a signal. A deadline is a signal. Uncertainty is a signal. Stillness and warmth are signals in the other direction.

## Why alert gets stuck

Modern demand doesn't come in emergencies that end. It comes in a continuous stream of small unresolved things — emails, decisions, paperwork in a language you're learning, a school you don't yet understand. Each one is minor. Together they mean alert never gets the "threat over" signal. The setting that was meant to be temporary becomes the default.

You can be safe, on a terrace in Antibes, with nothing wrong, and your body is running the emergency program at low volume. That's wired and tired. That's can't-switch-off. That's most of what walks through my door.

## What the body needs to switch

Not reasoning. You can't think your way out of alert; the setting doesn't take instructions from the mind. It takes evidence: bodily signals of safety, held for long enough to believe. Stillness. Warmth. Slow contact. Another calm human's attention. No demand. If those are present for ten or fifteen minutes, the body starts to switch on its own. That's the drop people describe.

## Where a session fits

A Reiki session is 45 minutes of exactly those signals, delivered on purpose. Lying down, fully clothed, hands resting lightly on the body, nothing asked — not to relax, not to breathe correctly, not to think of nothing. The body is simply given every reason to switch, and somewhere around minute ten it usually does.

That's the mechanism I can explain, and it needs no belief. There may be more to it; I think there is; you don't have to agree.

One session shows the body the switch. Four over a month — The Renewal — is where the body starts to find the switch itself, on a Tuesday, without a session.

If alert has become something a doctor should see — panic, chest symptoms, sleep gone entirely — that's the first conversation. Reiki is complementary; it works alongside care, never instead.

## Why "just relax" doesn't work

Telling someone in alert to relax adds a demand — now they're failing at relaxing as well as everything else. The nervous system can't be instructed. This is why meditation apps help some people and make others more anxious; the ones who find it hard are being asked to produce a state they don't have access to. A session removes the instruction entirely. You aren't asked to do anything, including relax. That absence is the whole method.

## FAQ

**What is nervous system regulation?**
The body's ability to move between alert and rest as needed. Dysregulation is getting stuck in alert — tired but wired, can't switch off — which is what most modern stress actually is.

**What is fight-or-flight, simply?**
The alert setting: faster heart, shorter breath, tense muscles, narrowed attention. Useful briefly; harmful when it becomes the default.

**How does Reiki regulate the nervous system?**
By providing 45 minutes of the bodily signals that switch it to rest — stillness, warmth, calm attention, no demand. The body responds to the conditions, not to belief.

## If your default setting has been alert too long

One session, €180, to show the body the switch. The Renewal, four for €640, to help it find the switch itself. Message me on WhatsApp — at your home or my space in Cannes.

title: Reiki for Athletes and Yacht Crew on the Riviera: Recovery Between Seasons
meta_title: Reiki for Athletes and Yacht Crew on the Riviera
meta_description: Reiki for athletes and yacht crew — recovery for bodies worked fifteen hours a day, muscle vs nervous-system fatigue, sessions on changeover days.
body:
Athletes and yacht crew have the same problem from opposite directions: a body that's used hard, on a schedule, with no real off. The athlete trains, competes, recovers on a plan — and the nervous system never gets the memo that the season has a pause in it. Crew work fifteen-hour days in July and August, sleep in a cabin, and are "on" from the moment a guest wakes. Both know how to rest a muscle. Neither, usually, knows how to rest the system running it.

I work with both on the Riviera — Monaco and Cap d'Antibes have a lot of one, the port at Antibes a lot of the other. Here's what a session does for a body that's fit and exhausted at the same time.

## Physical fatigue versus system fatigue

Physical fatigue is muscle. Rest, sleep, food and physio fix it, and athletes are good at all of those. System fatigue is different: the alert setting stuck on. Sleep is short and light even after a hard day. Recovery takes longer than it used to. Small things irritate. The body is doing everything right and still isn't fully restoring — because the repair setting, the parasympathetic one, isn't getting a proper turn.

Crew describe it as "I can sleep eight hours and wake up already done." Athletes describe it as a plateau nothing explains.

## What a session is, for a working body

Forty-five minutes lying down, fully clothed. Hands resting lightly on the body, head to feet, in a set sequence. Nothing asked — no stretching, no breathing to get right, no talking. For a body that's used to being told what to do with itself, this is unfamiliar and, most people tell me, the point. Somewhere around minute ten the system drops. Fifteen-hour days for eight weeks is a nervous system that hasn't been off since June. I work with captains who book it for their crew, and with crew who book it for themselves.

Between competitions, when the training load drops and the body is supposed to rebuild. A session then, or two a week apart, lets the rebuild actually happen instead of running at half speed under a system that's still in competition mode. Before a competition, the evening before, for the same reason executives use it before a board — to arrive as yourself rather than braced.

Book it for the crew on changeover day and don't tell them it's Reiki — call it a rest hour and let them find out. The ones who'd have refused on principle are the ones who sleep hardest. I've done this for crews of six in an afternoon, twenty minutes each in a spare cabin. By the time the next guests board, the boat feels different, and the guests notice without knowing why.

title: Energy Healing for Couples: One Session, Two Nervous Systems
meta_title: Energy Healing for Couples: Two Nervous Systems
meta_description: Energy healing for couples — why two people who moved abroad run each other's stress, and what back-to-back sessions at home do that talking doesn't.
body:
Two people who move abroad together end up running each other's stress. One is braced about the business; the other reads it before breakfast and braces too. One isn't sleeping; the other lies awake beside them. By month six each is carrying their own alert and the other person's, and the arguments are about the dishwasher because the real thing has no words yet.

Energy healing for couples, as I do it, isn't a joint ritual or a session where you hold hands. It's two sessions, back to back, in the same house on the same afternoon — each person 45 minutes on their own, with the other one somewhere else. The reason it works as a couple's thing is that two nervous systems that have been feeding each other's alert both stand down within the same two hours, and the house they come back to is a different house.

## Why one settled person isn't enough

If one partner has a session and comes home calm to a partner who's still braced, the calm lasts about an evening. The braced one re-alerts the calm one by dinner. Couples describe this: "I felt great and then I walked in and it was gone." Two systems need to drop close together for the drop to hold.

## What the afternoon looks like

I come to the house — a villa in Mougins, an apartment on the Croisette, wherever you are. One of you lies down first: 45 minutes, fully clothed, hands resting lightly on the body, no conversation. The other goes for a walk, or sits on the terrace, or works — somewhere out of the room. Then you swap. Two hours in total. At the end, both of you have had the same experience separately, and neither had to manage the other through it.

I don't do joint sessions on the same table. Two people watching each other relax is two people not relaxing.

## What couples say afterwards

"We didn't argue that night." "We sat outside and neither of us checked a phone." One couple who'd moved from London for his job told me the strangest part was noticing they'd both been holding their breath around each other, and hadn't known.

I'm not a couples therapist. If the relationship is in trouble, that's a therapist's work and I'll say so. What I do is take two braced bodies and give them both, in the same afternoon, the experience of not being braced — which often lets the actual conversation happen later without the alert running underneath it.

## When it's most useful

The first months after a move, when both of you are carrying more than you say. After a hard stretch — a business crisis, an illness in the family, a bad year. Before a decision you need to make together. And, honestly, on a holiday that's supposed to be the two of you and has turned into logistics.

Reiki is complementary. It doesn't fix a relationship, doesn't replace therapy, and if either of you describes something a doctor should see, that comes first.

## When one of you is sceptical

Usually one is. That's fine — I'd say it's the normal arrangement. The sceptical partner doesn't have to believe anything; they have to lie down for 45 minutes while the other one takes a walk. Most of them fall asleep and are mildly annoyed about it afterwards. I've never once had the sceptical partner be the one who didn't want to do it again.

## FAQ

**How does Reiki work for couples?**
Two separate 45-minute sessions, back to back, in the same house — each person alone. Both nervous systems stand down within the same two hours, and the calm holds because neither re-alerts the other.

**Can you do a joint Reiki session for a couple?**
I don't. Two people watching each other relax is two people not relaxing. Back to back, separately, works far better.

**Is couples Reiki a substitute for couples therapy?**
No. It clears the alert state that makes real conversation hard; the conversation itself is therapy's job or yours.

## If you've been running each other's stress

Message me on WhatsApp with an afternoon when you're both home. Two sessions, €360 for the pair, at your house. Neither of you has to explain anything to the other first.

title: Reiki for Highly Sensitive People: When the World Is Too Loud
meta_title: Reiki for Highly Sensitive People (HSP)
meta_description: Reiki for highly sensitive people — why HSPs run on alert in a new country, what a quiet no-demand session gives, how I adjust the room and pace.
body:
If you're a highly sensitive person — and roughly one in five people are, by the research on the trait — moving to the Riviera does something specific to you. The light is beautiful and too bright. The Croisette in August is unbearable. Every new social situation costs three times what it costs the people around you, and nobody can see why you're tired. You process more, deeper, and with less filter, and a new country is an enormous amount to process.

I'm writing this because "HSP" is a term that gets searched a lot in France — *hypersensibilité* is a real conversation here — and because highly sensitive people are, in my experience, the ones who respond most to a session and the ones most often put off by how sessions are usually described.

## Why HSPs run on alert abroad

High sensitivity means a nervous system that takes in more — more light, sound, subtext, other people's states — and processes it more thoroughly. That's an asset in a familiar place. In a new one, where everything is unfamiliar and there's no filter for what matters, it means the alert system is on all day. The préfecture, the school gate, the dinner with people you don't know yet: each one is a full processing event. By 6 pm the tank is empty and there's nothing left for the people you love.

## What most help gets wrong

Advice for HSPs tends to be about coping — boundaries, saying no, quiet time. Good, and not enough, because the tank doesn't refill from the absence of demand alone. It refills from a positive experience of safety: something the body reads as *you can stop processing now*. Most environments don't provide that. A dimmed room with a podcast is still input.

## What a session is, for someone sensitive

Forty-five minutes of no input. Lying down, fully clothed, in a room I've made quiet and dim if you'd like it — I'll ask. Hands resting lightly on the body; if touch is a lot for you, hands just above it, which works the same. No conversation. No music unless you want it. No scent. Nothing to read, respond to, or track.

Highly sensitive people drop faster than anyone I work with — often within five minutes — because the body has been waiting for exactly this. What people describe afterwards: "I didn't know I could feel that quiet." "It's the first time in months I wasn't processing something." "I could hear the sea and it wasn't too much."

## How I adjust

I ask about the room before I arrive: light, temperature, sound. I ask whether you'd rather hands on or just above. I keep the exchange before and after short — you don't need to perform being fine for me. And I don't fill the silence. For most clients that's a style; for sensitive clients it's the point.

## Over time

One session shows the body the quiet exists. Four over a month — The Renewal — is where it starts to be available on your own, and where the school gate stops costing what it costs. I'd start with one.

High sensitivity isn't a condition and doesn't need a doctor. But if what you're carrying has become anxiety that stops normal life, or exhaustion a doctor should look at, that comes first. Reiki is complementary — alongside, never instead.

## The exchange before and after

Most practitioners talk. I keep it short, and for sensitive people shorter still. Two questions at the door — how did you sleep, does anything hurt — and then the session. Afterwards, a minute of quiet before I say anything, then only what's useful. You don't have to describe your experience, rate it, or reassure me it was good. You can simply go back to sleep, and many do.

## FAQ

**Does Reiki work for highly sensitive people?**
In my experience, HSPs respond faster than anyone — the body has been waiting for a no-input environment. Sessions are adjusted for light, sound and touch.

**What if touch is too much for me?**
Hands rest just above the body instead of on it. It works the same, and many sensitive clients prefer it.

**Why is moving abroad so exhausting for an HSP?**
A sensitive nervous system processes everything more deeply, and a new country is all unfamiliar input. The alert system runs all day; the tank empties by evening.

## If the world has been too loud

Message me on WhatsApp and tell me what the room needs to be. One session, €180, at your home, adjusted for you. The exchange can be as short as you like.

title: Living with Chronic Pain: What Reiki Can and Can't Do Alongside Your Doctors
meta_title: Living with Chronic Pain: What Reiki Can and Can't Do
meta_description: Living with chronic pain and what Reiki can and can't do — not the cause, but the bracing around it and the sleep. Alongside your doctors, never instead.
body:
Chronic pain has two layers. The first is the pain itself — from a condition, an old injury, a nerve, a joint — and that's your doctors' territory, entirely. The second is everything the body does around the pain: the bracing against it, the shallow breath, the sleep that never gets deep because the body won't fully let go, the exhaustion of holding oneself carefully all day. Reiki doesn't touch the first layer. It works on the second, and for many people who've lived with pain for years, the second layer is a surprising proportion of what they're carrying.

I want that distinction clear before anything else, because chronic pain attracts more false promises than almost anything, and the people living with it deserve better than one more.

## The bracing

When something has hurt for a long time, the body organises itself around it. Muscles near the site tense to protect it — and stay tense. Movement becomes cautious. Breath gets shallow because deep breath moves things. The nervous system runs on low alert, because pain is a threat and the threat never ends. This layer isn't the pain, but it makes the pain feel larger, and it's exhausting in its own right.

People with chronic pain describe not remembering what it's like to fully rest. That's this layer.

## What a session does

Forty-five minutes at your home — I'll ask how you can lie comfortably and adapt to it; side, propped, whatever the pain allows. Fully clothed. Hands resting lightly on or above the body, and I stay away from anywhere touch hurts unless you and your doctor say it's fine. Nothing pressed. Nothing asked.

What people describe: the bracing letting go — the shoulders and jaw first, then the breath — and then a rest deeper than they've had in a long time. The pain is often still there. It's held by a body that isn't fighting it, and most people say it feels smaller and more contained for hours or days after. Sleep that night is the thing most often reported.

## What one client noticed

A woman with long-standing back and neck pain, seen by every relevant specialist, came for the tension around it. After a few sessions she said the pain hadn't gone — she hadn't expected it to — but the ease of movement had come back between sessions, and she'd stopped holding her breath when she turned her head. That's what this is for.

## What I won't say

That Reiki reduces pain — I don't know that it does, and the honest claim is that it reduces the bracing. That it addresses the cause — it doesn't. That you can change any medication, appointment or treatment — you can't, and if a session ever seems to conflict with your doctors' advice, they win. Reiki is complementary. It sits beside pain management; it isn't pain management.

## Over time

One session shows whether your bracing responds. Some people come weekly for a month. Some come monthly as maintenance, alongside everything else they do. The right rhythm is the one where the body stays a little less braced between sessions.

## The sleep part

If you've lived with pain for years, you know that sleep is where it does its worst — the position that hurts, the waking at 3 am, the exhaustion the next day that makes the pain feel bigger. Most people tell me the first thing that changes with sessions isn't the pain; it's the sleep. They go deeper, wake less, and the day after has more in it. Pain that's met by a rested body is a different experience from pain that's met by an exhausted one. That's not a small difference, and it's one I'll stand behind.

## FAQ

**Can Reiki help with chronic pain?**
It works on the bracing around pain — tension, shallow breath, poor sleep — not the pain's cause. People report the pain feeling more contained and sleep improving. It doesn't replace pain management.

**Is Reiki safe if I have a chronic pain condition?**
Yes — light hand contact, nothing pressed, position adapted to what you can manage. Tell your doctor you're having sessions, and keep every treatment.

**How often should I have Reiki for chronic pain?**
One to see if the bracing responds; then weekly for a month or monthly as maintenance, alongside your medical care.

Message me on WhatsApp and tell me what your doctors are doing and how you're able to lie. One session, €180, at your home. If the timing or the condition means a doctor should be asked first, I'll say so.
